items.title: Delta: Train that keeps disappearing; Ujevwu-Itakpe and the people left waiting
items.description: By Akpokona Omafuaire At Ujevwu, the railway tracks remain. Steel lines stretch into the distance, cutting through the landscape like a promise that was supposed to endure. The station stands as a symbol of modern transportation and of a government investment that was expected to connect communities, open new economic opportunities and give travellers an alternative to Nigeria’s often difficult roads. But there is a question that has become increasingly difficult to ignore: Where is the train? For the people who depend on the Ujevwu–Itakpe corridor, the railway story is no longer simply about the construction of tracks or the commissioning of infrastructure. It is about reliability. It is about safety. It is about livelihoods. And, increasingly, it is about waiting. The Itakpe–Warri standard-gauge railway, which includes the Ujevwu station, was completed and commissioned in 2020, 33 years after construction began. The Federal Government presented the 327-kilometre line as an important addition to Nigeria’s modern rail network. Commercial freight operations also began on the corridor in 2021. For communities along the route, however, the true value of a railway cannot be measured by kilometres of track. It is measured by whether the train arrives. And whether passengers can trust that it will arrive tomorrow. A promise interrupted The Warri–Itakpe Train Service has experienced a succession of disruptions. In February 2025, operations were halted because of a technical fault and later resumed. In April, the Nigerian Railway Corporation suspended full services after technical and operational problems, including engine failures, affected operations. The NRC said additional time was needed to introduce safety redundancies, improve equipment safety standards and undertake procedural upgrades. Then came another prolonged interruption. In August 2025, the NRC said urgent and critical track repairs were necessary to guarantee passenger safety, reliability and comfort. The corporation later announced that services would resume on October 29 after repairs, maintenance and system checks on the track and rolling stock. Operations were initially scheduled with seven coaches and temporary speed restrictions for safety monitoring. For passengers, the return of the train should have represented a return to normalcy. Instead, the corridor encountered another setback. Just days after the October resumption, a train derailed near Agbor. The NRC suspended services to allow a comprehensive safety and security audit. The corporation subsequently said preliminary investigations pointed to suspected track vandalism, and it announced the arrest of two suspects. The service eventually returned. But the cycle of interruption was not over. Then came 2026. In May 2026, the NRC again suspended the Warri–Itakpe service. This time, the corporation cited operational exigencies and technical advice from its engineers. It said the suspension was necessary to carry out critical operational assessments aimed at ensuring safety, reliability and improved service delivery. The service resumed again in January 2026 after another delay, with the NRC announcing scheduled operations between Ujevwu and Itakpe. But one of the most serious incidents came on June 8, 2026. A Warri–Itakpe train travelling from Itakpe derailed near Owa-Oyibu in Delta State. According to the NRC’s preliminary report, the train was carrying 482 people—442 passengers and 40 operational personnel. Four people died and 64 were injured The NRC said five coaches, one locomotive and a power car were affected, with three coaches and the power car overturning. The tragedy inevitably changed the conversation. It was no longer simply about delayed trains or inconvenient suspensions. It was about whether the railway could consistently deliver the most basic promise of public transportation: to take people to their destination safely. What caused the derailment? This question remains important because the answer is not yet final. The NRC’s August 2026 preliminary report said its internal investigation found a possible sudden bogie or wheel defect while the train was in motion. It also said the possible manner of brake application may have contributed to the severity of the incident. But the corporation stressed that these were working hypotheses, not definitive findings. An independent investigation by the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau is ongoing, and the final report remains pending. Significantly, the NRC said its investigators found no evidence of track vandalism at the June crash site. That distinction matters The corporation had previously attributed two incidents on the same service in November 2025 to track vandalism. The June 2026 incident, however, is being investigated on a different basis. The track has since been recovered and restored, according to the NRC. But the corporation says the locomotives are undergoing reconditioning and that service resumption will depend on detailed track and equipment safety audits. And Ujevwu waits This is where the statistics become human. For passengers, traders and residents around Ujevwu, every suspension has consequences. A railway station is rarely just a place where trains stop. It can support a small economy of food sellers, transport operators, traders, ticket agents and other informal businesses. Passengers who arrive at a station buy food, drinks and other necessities. Commercial transport operators carry passengers to and from the station. Businesses emerge around the movement of people. When the train stops, that movement stops with it. The question therefore extends beyond the railway itself: What happens to the people whose livelihoods have become connected to the railway? Reports from the resumption of service at Ujevwu in late 2025 captured renewed calls from stakeholders for the Federal Government to procure more trains, with the argument that rail could reduce pressure on Nigerians travelling by road. That demand points to another contradiction. Nigeria needs more dependable public transportation. Yet the railway that should provide part of that alternative has itself experienced repeated interruptions. Is this abandonment? To say that government has abandoned the Ujevwu–Itakpe corridor would require more evidence than a series of service interruptions. The government and the NRC have continued to repair the line, investigate incidents and announce plans for safer operations. The NRC’s latest report specifically says the corporation is committed to strengthening railway safety, improving operational resilience and restoring public confidence. The unanswered question Perhaps the most revealing thing about Ujevwu is that the railway itself has never disappeared. The tracks are still there. The station is still there. The investment is still there. What keeps disappearing is the certainty that the train will be there when people need it. That is why the story of Ujevwu–Itakpe cannot be reduced to a question of whether government built a railway. It did. The more difficult question is whether government can sustain it. Can the authorities provide reliable services? Can the railway be maintained properly? Can passengers travel without fear? Can vandalism be prevented? Can technical failures be addressed before they become emergencies? Can the people whose lives and businesses depend on the corridor plan their lives around a timetable they can trust? Until those questions are answered consistently, Ujevwu will remain a place of waiting. Waiting for the train. Waiting for reliability. Waiting for safety. Vanguard News The post Delta: Train that keeps disappearing; Ujevwu-Itakpe and the people left waiting appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Kouloub Faitah, nouvelle ministre déléguée chargée des Relations avec le Parlement et la Société civile
items.description: Kouloub Faitah, que le Roi Mohammed VI a nommée, vendredi, ministre déléguée auprès de la Cheffe du gouvernement, chargée des Relations avec le Parlement et la Société civile, est avocate au Barreau de Tanger. Titulaire d'une Licence en Droit privé et d'un Master en sciences criminelles et études sur la sécurité à l’Université Abdelmalek Essaâdi, Mme Faitah dispose d’une expérience juridique, parlementaire et associative. Elle est spécialisée notamment en droit de la famille et en affaires sociales, civiles et commerciales, en conseil et accompagnement juridiques, ainsi qu’en étude, préparation et suivi des dossiers judiciaires. Députée de la région de Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceïma (2021-2026), Mme Faitah a notamment occupé le poste de première vice-présidente de la Commission de la justice, de la législation, des droits de l’Homme et des libertés à la Chambre des représentants, et a siégé en tant que membre à la Commission thématique temporaire de l'égalité et de la parité. items.title: Bawumia will become President, Ghanaian youth stand to benefit – Ekua Amoakoh
items.description: Spokesperson for NPP flagbearer Dr Mahamudu Bawumia and the New Patriotic Party’s (NPP) Health Committee, Dr Ekua Amoakoh, says she believes Dr Bawumia will eventually become President of Ghana. She has also warned that it would be unfortunate for young people if the country misses the opportunity to benefit from his leadership. Speaking in a personality profile interview on JoyNews’ PM Express with Emefa Adeti, Dr Amoakoh expressed confidence in Dr Bawumia’s political future when asked whether she believed he would ever become president. “I do believe so. And I do believe that it will be very unfortunate for the young people of this country if it misses him,” she said. Dr Amoakoh also criticised the National Democratic Congress (NDC) for what she described as its efforts to portray Dr Bawumia negatively, including branding him a liar. She argued that political promises should be assessed consistently across parties rather than used selectively to attack opponents. “You might have heard a lot. You know, the NDC can even go as far as calling him a liar. If we want to call people liars, then we’ll call all of you liars,” she said. She cited the proposed Hope City project, which former President John Mahama pledged during his first administration, arguing that its non-fulfilment did not automatically make him a liar. “President Mahama promised to build Hope City in his first administration. He didn’t do it. Now he’s not even mentioning it again. Do I call him a liar for that? No,” she said. Dr Amoakoh accused the NDC of focusing on issues it could use against Dr Bawumia rather than engaging with his policy proposals and leadership record. Her remarks reflect the continuing political contest between the NPP and the governing NDC over their respective records and public claims. Dr Amoakoh said Dr Bawumia demonstrated a strong desire to work and address problems during his time as Vice President. She argued that his conduct in office suggested he would take a more active approach if elected president and given greater executive authority. “This is somebody that would have been vice president, and he would be, my own is go to church, go to this mosque, go for this wedding, go for this party, and he’ll be chilling in his office. He didn’t do that. It looked like he was itching to do stuff,” she said. She added that she expected his leadership to produce a different approach to governance if he became president. “So you can imagine if he has full control of it. So I always believe that we will probably see something different if we allow Dr Bawumia,” she said.

items.title: LHC extends stay against deportation of Afghan students
items.description: LAHORE: The Lahore High Court on Friday extended a stay against expulsion and deportation of Afghan medical students and granted the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) more time to submit its reply. Justice Khalid Ishaq heard the petitions filed by over 30 Afghan students, including Syed Mubeenul Fatti, challenging the PMDC notifications. A counsel for the PMDC told the court that the prime minister office had issued a direction to the relevant authorities to allow the Afghan students to continue their studies subject to valid visa and immigration requirements. When the judge asked about the written reply, the counsel sought time to submit it. The judge accepted the request and adjourned the hearing for a date to be fixed by the office. He also extended its order restraining the authorities from deporting the students. The petitioners stated that notifications for their deportation had been issued on July 31 and Sept 1. They challenged the notifications and asked the court to declare them illegal and set them aside. The court had on Sept 11 suspended the operation of the PMDC directives ordering Afghan medical students to return to the neighbouring country. Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

items.title: 2027: Why Tinubu’s challengers are struggling to unite
items.description: * Tinubu may win without unity of opposition — Ben Obi; Timing of negotiations is a major obstacle — Adebayo; Adds opposition woke up late; Olawepo-Hashim frowns at lumping all opposition together As opposition leaders intensify consultations ahead of the 2027 presidential election, rival ambitions, ideological differences and disagreements over candidate selection continue to complicate efforts to build a common front against President Bola Tinubu. LUMINOUS JANNAMIKE examines the obstacles confronting the opposition and the prospects for a united challenge. Nigeria’s opposition leaders are united in their desire to challenge President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 presidential election, but translating that common purpose into a workable political alliance remains a more complicated task, with competing presidential ambitions, ideological differences and uncertainty over candidate selection threatening to undermine ongoing negotiations. On Wednesday, President Tinubu inaugurated a coalition Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, including members from the Accord Party; All Progressives, Grand Alliance, APGA; and Peoples Democratic Party, PDP. The three opposition parties were represented in the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, campaign team via Governor Ademola Adeleke of Osun State (Accord Party); Governor Chukwuma Soludo of Anambra (APGA); and Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Minister, Chief Nyesom Wike(PDP). The APC, apparently, appears to have done first what the opposition is expected to do. Promoters of the coalition of leading opposition parties presidential candidates such as Alhaji Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress, ADC; Mr Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC; Engr Seyi Makinde of the Allied Peoples Movement, APM; Mr Donald Duke of the Peoples Redemption Party, PRP; and Prince Adewale Adebayo of the Social Democratic Party, SDP. While consultations among opposition parties have revived hopes of a common front, the central questions remain unanswered: who will lead the proposed coalition, how will the candidate emerge, and what guarantees will persuade other aspirants to accept the outcome? The challenge is not merely to bring political leaders into the same room, but to secure an agreement that can withstand the pressures of presidential ambition, party interests and the struggle for control of a joint campaign. From declarations to commitments The Director of Media and Publicity of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Kola Ologbondiyan, told Saturday Vanguard that the opposition still has an opportunity to reach an arrangement before the election. “I strongly believe that the opposition can mount a credible challenge to President Tinubu before the January 2027 election. And my belief is based on the decision reached at the meeting held in Ibadan among all the opposition political parties to look at that proposed grand alliance. The decision reached by the majority of the opposition parties was that, at the nick of time, they were going to pull together,” he said. Ologbondiyan expressed confidence that the parties could still realign, despite the disagreements and political movements that have complicated efforts to build a common platform. His optimism comes amid renewed consultations involving six opposition parties and presidential candidates, including Atiku Abubakar, Obi, Seyi Makinde, Donald Duke and Adewole Adebayo, over a framework for cooperation ahead of the 2027 polls. The consultations followed calls for sustained dialogue and coordinated action among opposition parties. Yet, agreement to continue talking is different from an agreement on who should emerge as the coalition’s presidential candidate. Tinubu may win without unity of opposition —Ben Obi Senator Ben Obi, who told Saturday Vanguard that he had taken it upon himself to facilitate discussions among leading opposition figures, believes the consequences of failure could be significant. “I believe very strongly that if the opposition does not come together, the incumbent might coast to victory. So, I gave myself an assignment,” Senator Obi said. “Seyi Makinde is like my younger brother, just as Peter Obi is. Atiku is my boss and my friend, and we are like one family. So, I approached the three of them and took time to work things out with them. “I said to myself that if the opposition did not come together, we would be wasting our time.” Obi said he initiated discussions among Makinde, Peter Obi and Atiku, asking each of them to nominate two trusted associates to participate in a six-person committee. He subsequently approached former Ekiti State Governor Kayode Fayemi to coordinate the meetings. “I told Kayode Fayemi, ‘Don’t allow the meeting to die,’” Obi said. “They will not agree to step down for anybody. But, from the way I see things, we may reach a stalemate (at the polls in January, 2027). If that happens, this committee could become the answer.” Whether the committee can help resolve that dilemma will depend on its mandate, the willingness of the principals to accept its recommendations and the extent to which any eventual understanding becomes binding. Ambition meets ideology For Comrade Mark Adebayo, Chief Communications Adviser to the Adebayo-Bugaje Presidential Campaign, who spoke to Saturday Vanguard, the timing of the negotiations is itself a major obstacle. “I think the biggest obstacle to such a possibility (of a united front) is the time factor,” Adebayo said. “The conversations around different political Parties coming together to support a single presidential ticket came too late in the day, in my opinion. That’s a conversation that should have begun at least three years ago by building critical political infrastructures to achieve that. You can’t start such a crucial process on the eve of a general election.” Opposition woke up late Adebayo argued that a coalition requires more than last-minute consultations, pointing to the need for political structures capable of sustaining joint mobilisation and translating agreements among leaders into coordinated action across the country. He also identified ideological differences among the parties and their presidential candidates as a fundamental obstacle. “Secondly, the differences in political and governance ideologies of the various Parties and candidates would also constitute fundamental obstacles to such possibility,” he said. “I think the opposition woke up to that realization too late. Meanwhile, while I agree it is extremely challenging, it is not impossible for one presidential candidate to defeat the incumbent.” Adebayo said a successful challenge would require extensive mobilisation around a common political programme, adding that Prince Adewole Adebayo was working towards that objective. His position raises a question that extends beyond the timing of the negotiations: how much ideological agreement is necessary for opposition parties to work together? Gbenga Olawepo-Hashim, the Accord Party presidential candidate, has drawn a distinction between his political outlook and those of Atiku and Obi, arguing that opposition politicians should not automatically be treated as members of the same ideological bloc simply because they oppose the ruling party. Olawepo-Hashim frowns at lumping all opposition together Speaking on Seun Okinbaloye’s Mic On Podcast, Olawepo-Hashim said: “There are opposition candidates who share the left-centre ideology, more welfarists, more sympathetic, more compassionate to the common people. Sowore, Adebayo and I belong to that. So we shouldn’t be lumped together.” Olawepo-Hashim described himself, Omoyele Sowore of the African Action Congress and Adewole Adebayo of the Social Democratic Party as sharing a left-centre, welfarist orientation. He placed Atiku and Obi in what he described as the extreme conservative political wing, particularly in relation to economic policy and petrol subsidy. When asked whether the three politicians had formed an alliance, he replied on the podcast: “We already did. We signed it in Port Harcourt, and it was in the public space.” The agreement, involving the Accord, AAC and SDP presidential candidates, represents a distinct initiative from the broader consultations among opposition parties. Its existence does not, in itself, establish that the wider opposition has agreed on a joint presidential ticket. The distinction also illustrates the competing approaches to cooperation. While some leaders are exploring a broad arrangement that could bring different political tendencies together, Olawepo-Hashim has emphasised the importance of shared ideological ground. The unresolved question is whether parties with different economic philosophies can agree on a limited common programme while retaining their individual identities, or whether such differences will become another source of disagreement when the negotiations reach substantive policy questions. Who leads, and on what terms? Beyond ideology, the opposition must settle the practical details that determine whether a coalition can function as a single political force. The first is candidate selection. A credible arrangement would require an agreed process for choosing a presidential candidate, whether through consensus, a negotiated formula or another mechanism acceptable to the participating parties. The second is the treatment of unsuccessful candidates. Senator Obi’s account suggests that persuading leading contenders to step aside may be difficult, making it necessary to establish in advance how disagreements will be resolved and what commitments participants will make to support the eventual candidate. Power-sharing presents another challenge. Decisions on the running mate, joint campaign leadership, funding, messaging and grassroots mobilisation could become contentious unless the parties agree on clear responsibilities and decision-making procedures. There is also the question of whether the parties can sustain cooperation beyond the negotiations themselves. A coalition that announces a common purpose but retains separate campaign commands, competing messages and conflicting political priorities could struggle to demonstrate that its agreement amounts to more than an understanding among leaders. Ologbondiyan’s expectation that opposition parties could pull together at a decisive moment and Senator Obi’s account of efforts to prevent the talks from collapsing offer two perspectives on the same challenge. Adebayo, meanwhile, warns that the necessary political groundwork should have begun much earlier. Taken together, their accounts show that the opposition’s task is not simply to agree that Tinubu should be challenged, but to determine how that challenge will be organised and who will exercise authority within it. Vanguard News The post 2027: Why Tinubu’s challengers are struggling to unite appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Imaginary justice
items.description: ON any given day, newspaper headlines across Pakistan are littered with updates on court cases. These usually fall into two categories. The first are updates on cases involving political leaders in prison: so and so is brought out for a hearing, so and so has a case stayed. The second category comprises criminal cases that have, largely owing to social media, attracted some attention. Many involve female victims who were killed or raped, sometimes both. Dead women are a topic of interest in Pakistan — much more so than living women. There is, however, a third category of cases. These belong to ordinary people — everyday folk who, often erroneously, imagine that Pakistan’s court system can actually deliver justice. The statistics are alarming. According to the Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan, more than 2.2 million cases were pending in Pakistani courts at the end of December 2025. Most of these are civil cases, and if you are unlucky enough to have to file one, you may wait years, sometimes decades, for a final resolution. An entire generation can be conceived, born and raised before your inheritance dispute with your siblings is resolved. According to one research paper that analysed the backlog, reasons for delays include frequent adjournments, shortages of judicial officers, inadequate process serving, improper working environments, poor record-keeping facilities, and few resources to run the courts. Justice, obviously, is not a priority for Pakistan’s rulers. It is not surprising then that the World Justice Project, which issues an annual report on the rule of law in various countries, ranked Pakistan 130th out of 143 countries in 2025. Pakistan was thus among the 14 lowest-ranked countries for adherence to the rule of law. Accountability, quite obviously, is a fantasy. The situation, and the mental picture of thousands and thousands of files piled high with millions of people awaiting justice, is reminiscent of Charles Dickens’ Bleak House, which tells the story of a case that went on for decades. Portions of the opening paragraph read: “Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.” Fog in Dickens’ narrative stands not simply for the weather phenomenon but also for the murky opacities of a convoluted justice system. More appropriately, a parallel could be drawn with the smog that often settles over Pakistani cities. Smog — a consequence of environmental impurities and societal apathy — has nowhere to go so it suspends itself over human life and can be enumerated in the millions of untended files pushed from hearing to hearing. Sometimes a judge is unavailable, sometimes the lawyers are absent. The emphasis is on everyone except the poor, hapless souls who imagined that justice was a possibility. The smog, of course, is a metaphor, but it points to lived truths about life in Pakistan. If you are an ordinary person, you live a life on the defensive. When you leave your house, you carry only hope and a prayer. If something goes wrong — your parked car gets hit by a passing truck, your phone is stolen, someone attacks you — you realise just how vulnerable you are. No one will replace your car or your phone, and if your attacker can bribe law enforcers with a bigger pile of cash than you can offer to have them file an FIR, then no one will care about that either. Accountability, quite obviously, is a fantasy. All this illustrates how the inability to count on a fu­­nctioning le­­g­al system creates a con­­tor- ted society that functions ac­­c­ording to the crudest calculations of po­­w­­er. The inability to obtain justice does not simply impede your ability to recover money owed to you or resolve an inheritance dispute. It also means that in any interaction, calculations are made about who has more power and who has less. If a middle-class person has the misfortune of getting into a dispute with someone very wealthy, it is not law that will determine the outcome; it is power. Solutions like model courts and alternative dispute resolution mechanisms have been thrown at the problem. These have not resolved the underlying structural weaknesses. Pakistan’s courts do not fail simply because there is a need for more courts or another mechanism for resolving disputes. They fail, the argument goes, because powerful Pakistanis — those who draw their power from wealth or brute force — do not believe in the rule of law. The consequence is a legal system that serves as a gloss to disguise the crimes of the powerful while the weak remain cowed and tortured by the failures of a sham system. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy. rafia.zakaria@gmail.com Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

items.title: Ekua Amoakoh explains how Bawumia’s policy ideas drew her closer to NPP before 2024 elections
items.description: Spokesperson for NPP flagbearer Dr Mahamudu Bawumia and the New Patriotic Party’s (NPP) Health Committee, Dr Ekua Amoakoh, says a briefing by Dr Bawumia helped convince her to become more committed to the party ahead of the 2024 general elections. She said she had been largely detached from the NPP before taking up research into its health sector record, but her findings and an encounter with Dr Bawumia changed her perspective. Speaking in a personality profile interview on JoyNews’ PM Express with Emefa Adeti, Dr Amoakoh said her limited political engagement at the time was reflected in her social media activity. “Ahead of 2024, I wasn’t really interested in the NPP too much. Even if you want to go back and look at my social media, I was not even writing anything NPP or doing anything. I was just detached. There was like a disconnection,” she said. Dr Amoakoh said her involvement in research into the party’s health sector performance gave her a different view of its record. “But then when I started going to do the research, I saw how much we had actually achieved,” she said. She said her interest deepened after attending a briefing by Dr Bawumia to party communicators shortly before the launch of the NPP’s manifesto. “After I listened to him that day, I was like, ‘Okay, I think I see what these people are on about. There’s something there.’ He looked like he was very passionate about solving problems,” she recounted. Dr Amoakoh said she was particularly impressed by Dr Bawumia’s account of how he approached policy challenges, including the domestic gold purchase programme. She described his ability to devise unconventional solutions to economic problems as one of the qualities that drew her towards his leadership. “He was talking about how he came up with the domestic gold purchase programme, about how MTN needed some money. I thought that whole ability to think of something out of the box to fix a problem was maybe the type of person whose leadership could get us to a point of some prosperity,” she said. Her comments reflect her personal assessment of Dr Bawumia’s policy approach and the influence it had on her political commitment. Dr Amoakoh argued that Ghana needed leadership focused not only on tackling corruption but also on deliberately creating the conditions for economic growth and prosperity. “I don’t think it’s just punishing corruption. It’s also being intentional about generating prosperity,” she said. She cited South Korea and China as examples of countries that pursued approaches she believes helped accelerate their economic development. She said Ghana appeared to be progressing more slowly than countries that had once faced comparable economic challenges. “If you look at Ghana, it looks like we are marking time. We’re walking slowly when we could have been maybe galloping or jumping at the pace of Singapore and all the other countries,” she said. Dr Amoakoh also argued that Ghana needed leaders who could set out a clear strategy for generating wealth and expanding economic opportunities. Her remarks offer insight into the considerations that shaped her political involvement ahead of the 2024 elections and her support for Dr Bawumia’s approach to governance. Dr Amoakoh made the comments during her personality profile interview on JoyNews’ PM Express with Emefa Adeti.

items.title: Kathleen Belew, historiadora: “Trump utiliza y se beneficia de los supremacistas blancos”
items.description: Patrick Crusius, un joven retraído de 21 años, condujo nueve horas desde las afueras de Dallas hasta El Paso, en la frontera entre México y Estados Unidos. Tras viajar toda la noche, tomó el volante durante una hora más sin rumbo fijo hasta que aparcó el coche al exterior de un Walmart. Pasadas las diez y media de la mañana, publicó un manifiesto en un foro de internet en el que advertía de “una invasión hispana de Texas” y sacó de su maletero un rifle semiautomático. Crusius mató a 23 personas e hirió a otras 22 víctimas, la mayoría de origen mexicano. Aquel 3 de agosto de 2019 se produjo el ataque racista más letal que ha sufrido la comunidad latina en suelo estadounidense . Seguir leyendo

items.title: A los ricos no les basta con la piscina: las zonas comunes se adaptan al gusto del comprador extranjero en los edificios de ultralujo
items.description: Si para muchos españoles tener una piscina en casa ya es un lujo, a los ricos parece que les sabe a poco. Dentro de las comodidades que ofrecen los nuevos edificios de ultralujo en Madrid, las piletas han pasado a un segundo plano, son un elemento que se da por hecho o, incluso, se prescinde de ellas para dejar espacio a otros amenities , término que se usa en el sector inmobiliario para referirse a los servicios comunes de un edificio. En unos años en los que ya no es descabellado hablar de 20.000 euros por metro cuadrado, e incluso 30.000 euros en ciertos proyectos singulares, en las zonas más prémium de la ciudad, los productos a la venta se han ido refinando y adecuándose a los gustos de los compradores extranjeros que han puesto sus ojos en la capital. Seguir leyendo De la pinacoteca a la cámara de crioterapia en las mansiones El equipamiento de las mansiones en España cambia según la edad de quien las habite, recoge un informe de la aseguradora Hiscox. Mientras los boomers buscan hueco para sus colecciones de arte y un lugar para guardar las joyas de la familia, las generaciones más jóvenes transforman sus casas en centros de bienestar, con cámara de crioterapia incluida. “Hoy en día, es extraña la vivienda que no tiene una habitación dedicada al gimnasio con máquinas de última generación”, asegura Eva Peribáñez, directora de arte y clientes privados de Hiscox España. “Se ha pasado a que lucir lo que se tiene sea lo que da la posición social”, sostiene. Y pone como ejemplo los ascensores que permiten presumir de coche en el salón de la vivienda.

items.title: The real reset
items.description: IN times like this, we need people who tell hard truths while insisting that the present state of our politics is not permanent. On the one hand, White House aide Stephen Miller says that “we live in a world that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power”, and on the other, philosopher Hannah Arendt says that “out of the barrel of a gun grows the most effective command, resulting in the most instant and perfect obedience. What never can grow out of it is power”. In her 1970 book On Violence, Arendt stresses that violence is not a form of power but its opposite. According to her, power is collective, consensual and relational. By contrast, violence is instrumental and coercive; its strength evaporates the moment the threat is evaded or withdrawn. “Violence can always destroy power,” she concludes. Pakistan’s present rulers seem to follow Thucydides’ thought: “The strong do what they can, and the weak suffer what they must.” Against this backdrop, they want to reset the collapsed system of governance, according to the minister in charge of internal security and cricket affairs that show clear signs of deterioration. Instead of taking responsibility, he has blamed others for the system’s rot. During his tenure, the security situation in Balochistan and KP has deteriorated significantly. Moreover, widespread violence was witnessed in AJK before the recent polls there. The first move to reset the system was to promulgate governor’s rule and proclaim an indefinite emergency in a province where an opposition political party with strong public support had been in power since early 2024. The reasons given are couched in a security narrative. The KP government had failed to control the tide of terrorism since it was at the helm of affairs during the last two to three years. The TTP had unleashed terror in the province, especially in five key border districts on the Afghan border. Many tribal jirgas and multiparty forums held by the provincial legislature opposed the military operations and the use of drone technology that resulted in civilian casualties and population displacement. The protest march led by the chief minister was a political move to persuade the ruling elite to adhere to the Islamabad High Court and Supreme Court decisions to allow access to the incarcerated founder of their party. The SC had directed the prisoner to be treated in a private hospital, in the presence of his physicians and family members. Those court orders were flouted. A simple, humane gesture of following the court’s directions would have defused the political tension between the ruling elite and the opposition parties. Two mainstream parties have lost out the most in the KP fiasco: the PML-N and PPP. The security situation in Balochistan is far more daunting. Why is there no governor’s rule or emergency there? The security situation in Balochistan is far more daunting. There, the state faces an armed insurgency in Baloch-dominated areas. The number of terrorist incidents over the last two years is higher than in KP, and the level of violence against the state agencies, including the police, civil armed forces, and the military, is far more serious than anywhere else. Why is there no governor’s rule or emergency there? The answer is simple: the governing administration there is aligned with the establishment. A security strategy based on force has alienated the Baloch youth from the state. Even the Pakhtun areas close to the Afghan and KP borders are reeling under the onslaught of terrorist organisations that are exploiting internal fissures in the two provinces. Here, we must ask a basic question: what kind of governance structure should dominate Pakistan? Should it be the constitutional order envisioned by the country’s founders, where every citizen is equal under the law, due process is respected, and all institutions act within their legal bounds? Or should Pakistan remain an eternal security state, where justice, lawmaking, foreign policy, the economy, and internal affairs are militarised? A state can justify its power in three ways: by promoting shared values rather than imposing a narrative; by ensuring the sanctity of the electoral process and the rule of law; and by establishing performance legitimacy. The present ruling elite struggles to pass this test. The current governance model needs a reset. Here is how to do it. First, true representation can emerge only through fair and free elections. A state machinery that cannot hold free elections loses credibility and citizens’ trust. Parliament must represent the people’s will. We need a new and independent election commission. Internal stability and cohesion will remain elusive if questions about the legitimacy of the ruling set-up persist. Only a renewed and fair public mandate at this stage can settle these questions. Second, centralised control must be replaced with genuine provincial autonomy and strong local self-government. We must adhere to the letter and spirit of the original 1973 Constitution, as the promise of provincial autonomy was the cornerstone of the near-consensus social contract between the state and society. Third, the independence of the judiciary must be restored by genuine representatives in the new parliament elected through fair mid-term polls. The judiciary’s role in upholding the rule of law and fair administration of justice is crucial to a democratic state. Fourth, our premier federal intelligence agencies appear to be operating outside the legal fra­m­ework. This lack of accountability must be ad­­d­ressed through parliamentary oversight and laws that clearly define the role of the agencies in both the internal and external security dimensions. Fifth, terrorism and violent extremism should be addressed by faithfully adhering to the updated CT NAP in 2021 through a long-term, sustainable strategy that invests in non-kinetic measures to address these challenges. Short-term kinetic military operations must be followed by multi-stakeholder, whole-of-society engagement strategies and action plans. Finally, a meaningful reset can happen only if the security state does not involve itself in political matters. The writer is a former police officer. Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

items.title: El PSOE se conjura en su comité federal para pelear por otra remontada electoral
items.description: El PSOE celebra este sábado un comité federal de trámite pese a su trascendencia orgánica porque ratificará las listas electorales al Congreso y el Senado para el 29-N. Ferraz ha reconvertido la reunión del principal órgano del partido entre congresos en un gran mitin , que se ha visto enturbiado a última hora tras la dimisión de la portavoz del partido, Montse Mínguez, tras las críticas por los negocios inmobiliarios de su pareja. El propósito de Pedro Sánchez es que el comité federal sirva de acicate a los socialistas, que como en 2023 están obligados a una nueva remontada imposible que ninguna casa de encuestas pronostica salvo el CIS. El cónclave ni siquiera se celebrará en la sede federal del PSOE, sino en Fuenlabrada, dentro de la estrategia que el equipo de campaña del presidente ha diseñado con decenas de actos en bastiones socialistas para movilizar a su electorado más apático y descontento con el Gobierno, sacarle de la abstención y convencerle para que acuda a las urnas y hacer posible otra misión imposible. items.title: Del 15-M al 29-N: una conversación entre Ignacio Urquizu y Kiko Llaneras
items.description: “No queda ninguna duda de que efectivamente se ha producido un desplazamiento ideológico de los jóvenes hacia posiciones conservadoras”. Esta es la conclusión de Generación 15-M de Ignacio Urquizu (Alcañiz, 1976), un ensayo que ha cobrado inesperada actualidad. Tras la acampada en Sol (que se produce 15 años después de aquella a la que hace referencia el título del libro) y la convocatoria de elecciones generales, ahora llega la avalancha de los sondeos. En esta entrevista se analizan los cambios en profundidad que se deducen de los mejores datos disponibles. Ignacio Urquizu fue diputado por el PSOE y ha sido alcalde de su ciudad. Este profesor de sociología actualmente es el director de Metroscopia, empresa dedicada a investigar la opinión pública en España. items.title: Llega a los hospitales el cannabis medicinal: “Por fin dejamos de estar en manos de los narcos”
items.description: Los nuevos fármacos a base de cannabis empezarán a llegar a partir de la semana que viene a los hospitales españoles. Ha sido necesario un año, desde que se aprobó el real decreto que abrió esta vía , para que la Agencia Española del Medicamento (AEMPS) los regulara, los proveedores se inscribieran, se cerrara la distribución y que los centros comenzaran a hacer pedidos. Llegarán a los pacientes poco a poco, a medida que los médicos y las farmacias hospitalarias vayan familiarizándose con estos preparados. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Ganancias millonarias y subidas de precio: las farmacéuticas hacen caja en plena escasez de las hormonas para la menopausia
items.description: “Estamos aquí por la salud de la mujer”. “Nuestra misión: la salud y el bienestar de la mujer”. “Investigamos e innovamos con un objetivo prioritario: la salud integral de la mujer”. Las webs de los laboratorios que fabrican los tratamientos hormonales para la menopausia y para el tratamiento de las mujeres trans se parecen mucho entre sí. Las estanterías de las farmacias españolas, también. Desde marzo falta el spray de estradiol Lenzetto. Después, empezaron a escasear varios parches, dos comprimidos han desaparecido del mercado y, ahora, el único tratamiento transdérmico no en parches disponible , el gel Oestraclin, está sufriendo también problemas de escasez en lugares como Barcelona o Madrid, según han trasladado varias mujeres a este periódico. Esa aplicación transdérmica es la vía de aplicación preferida por los ginecólogos, ya que evita algunos de los problemas conocidos de las píldoras. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Saul Newman: “Si eres Elon Musk y lo has comprado todo, la única cosa que nos queda por venderte es escapar de la muerte”
items.description: Jiroemon Kimura llegó a ser el hombre más viejo del mundo. Cuando murió en 2013, había pasado sobre la Tierra 116 años y 54 días. El secreto de este anciano centenario japonés, decía, era hacer siempre comidas ligeras. Kimura tenía ocho hijos y una esposa. Y también tenía dos fechas de nacimiento oficiales y había terminado la educación primaria en tres años diferentes: 1907, 1909 y 1911. La historia se vuelve todavía un poco más rara, ya que algunos registros apuntan a que Jiroemon Kimura había reconocido en vida haber mentido sobre su edad. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La vida al límite de Rafa Botella, el abanderado de la ley de eutanasia
items.description: Rafa Botella lleva un tiempo meditando. Descubrió las filosofías orientales, el flujo natural del tao chino, y se volcó en su conocimiento. Su conversación discurre como una corriente continua, tranquila y reflexiva, incluso cuando recuerda sus años desenfrenados, las noches vertiginosas de música hardcore y drogas, entronizado como uno de los príncipes de la discoteca del momento, uno de los jóvenes más populares de su pueblo, Simat de la Valldigna, a 55 kilómetros de Valencia. Seguir leyendo

items.title: No todos los ultraprocesados son igual de malos para la salud: “Esta clasificación puede ocultar diferencias en los nutrientes”
items.description: Decía hace un tiempo la nutricionista Azahara Nieto que en las cosas del comer, es una práctica habitual “categorizar moralmente a los alimentos”. O buenos o malos, sanos o dañinos, sin medias tintas. Pero la cosa no es tan sencilla: “Ningún alimento, por muy sano que sea, va a mejorar sustancialmente nuestra salud, ya que la salud es un conjunto de factores que no solo tienen que ver con a la alimentación. Por la misma razón, un alimento no tan nutritivo no va a hacer que nuestra salud empeore. Todo es mucho más complejo, requiere de flexibilidad y equilibrio”, advertía en un artículo en EL PAÍS. En nutrición no sirven las consignas simplistas ni las etiquetas de brocha gorda y la ciencia no hace más que demostrarlo. El último ejemplo es un estudio recién publicado que cuestiona la idea instalada de que todos los alimentos ultraprocesados son igual de nocivos. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Las migajas
items.description: Una colega me envía un fragmento de la carta que le escribió Saul Bellow a Bette Howland, una escritora que había tomado pastillas para suicidarse y que contó esa experiencia en su libro S-3 , quizás siguiendo el consejo que le dio Bellow en aquella carta: “En cuanto a escribir, creo que deberías hacerlo, en la cama, y aprovechar tu infelicidad. Yo lo hago. Muchos lo hacen. Uno debería cocinar y comerse su miseria. Encadenarla como a un perro. Aprovecharla como si fueran las Cataratas del Niágara, para generar luz y suministrar voltaje para sillas eléctricas”. No siempre el sufrimiento puede capitalizarse, ni siquiera si se tiene talento. Allí está Silvia Plath, que abandonó la poesía para abrazar la muerte por gas. Por otra parte, el sufrimiento psíquico no es requisito para ser extraordinario, ni lo garantiza. En España, el 29% de los adultos presenta síntomas depresivos. Un 10% de la población consume antidepresivos a diario. La demanda de esos fármacos subió un 24% en el último año. Hace meses, en Madrid, una persona me preguntó qué podía hacerse para abordar el problema de la salud mental. Dije que hay dos palabras que se me ocurren: rápido y fácil. No que el tratamiento sea rápido y fácil, sino el acceso a él. Que no haya que esperar meses para una consulta, que la (falsa) solución no se reduzca a una pastilla. El gasto mundial destinado a este rubro representa apenas el 2% del presupuesto de salud. Ese es el voltaje de importancia que los países adjudican al tema. Una cifra miserable que condena a la mayoría a cocinar el sufrimiento en soledad, sin más recurso que la resistencia propia. Capitalizar el dolor no es una virtud artística, es un milagro del talento. Para el resto, es una calamidad cotidiana. Mientras la respuesta sea una lista de espera infinita o una pastilla automática, seguiremos encadenando el dolor como a un perro. Sólo que, tarde o temprano, es un perro que muerde.

items.title: Montse Minguez, ascenso y caída de la portavoz del PSOE
items.description: La diputada socialista Montserrat Minguez decidió este viernes dimitir y dar un paso al lado tras el vendaval de críticas de la oposición por informaciones sobre los negocios inmobiliarios de su pareja. Todo estaba destinado a que la también portavoz del PSOE fuera la cabeza de lista por Lleida para las elecciones del 29N, pero decidió a última hora renunciar a su fulgurante carrera política. “He tomado la decisión de dar un paso atrás convencida de que es lo mejor para el proyecto colectivo al que he dedicado mi esfuerzo, mi compromiso y mis mejores energías”, afirmó en un tuit publicado este viernes por la tarde que impactó y conmocionó a los miembros del Consell Nacional del PSC reunidos en la sede del partido para proclamar a los candidatos de Girona, Lleida y Tarragona. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Adiós a la vieja cárcel de San Sebastián, foco de represión franquista e inspiración de Kortatu
items.description: Una cárcel en calma no es una cárcel. La vieja prisión de Martutene está en silencio, no hay bullicio, tampoco se oyen avisos por la megafonía, ni retumba ya el eco metálico y sobrecogedor que produce el cierre de las celdas. Martutene ya no es una cárcel, pero conserva todos los elementos de un penal decadente : la garita central de los vigilantes, las galerías enrejadas donde vivieron los reclusos, un gran patio con frontón cubierto, los locutorios y las habitaciones para el vis a vis… Hay rejas por doquier, con unos pestillos de hierro deslizantes para garantizar la seguridad interior. En este lugar los calendarios se detuvieron en el mes de junio de 2026, cuando todos los internos (230 en total) fueron trasladados entonces al nuevo centro penitenciario de Gipuzkoa, ubicado en Zubieta. Martutene ya es historia. Antes de cambiar de prisión, una reclusa dejó escrita su despedida en la pared de la celda 9 de mujeres: “Adiós Martutene. Aquí estuve yo. Desde 2018 hasta hoy… 2026”. Y ahí seguirá el escrito, que firmó “La gata”, hasta que esta vieja cárcel de 78 años sea demolida para construir en el solar un polígono residencial de 400 viviendas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Vertidos kilométricos y fauna amenazada: las otras consecuencias de la escalada contra petroleros en el Mar Negro
items.description: El Mar Negro encadena un vertido tras otro por la guerra de Rusia contra Ucrania . Ucrania ataca la industria petrolera del Kremlin, una de sus principales fuentes de ingresos, y Rusia bombardea los transportes que cargan cereales y otros productos ucranios. Esta escalada ha recrudecido los problemas medioambientales de la cuenca marina, donde aún se filtra el crudo que cargaban otros dos viejos petroleros rusos que se hundieron hace casi dos años en una tormenta. Las playas de varias localidades turísticas costeras ya están sufriendo las consecuencias, con manchas de crudo que ensucian el paisaje y perjudican a las aves. Uno de los mayores navíos alcanzados en la última oleada de ataques ucranios cargaba hasta 100.000 toneladas de petróleo, aunque no hay estimaciones precisas de cuánto fuel se ha vertido al mar. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ‘Novecento’: aquel espectáculo que empleó 50 millones de dólares para explicar a Hollywood el comunismo
items.description: Un panfleto comunista rodado como una superproducción de Hollywood. Cine de autor para el público de masas. Y una historia épica sobre las relaciones íntimas de dos familias. Las contradicciones y el exceso definen Novecento (1976), monumental película de Bernardo Bertolucci que acaba de cumplir medio siglo. El cineasta quería hacer una epopeya de izquierdas, así que puso al servicio de los ideales marxistas una maquinaria de producción capitalista, un reparto de estrellas internacionales y una ambición narrativa más propia de un escritor del siglo XIX que de un militante comunista moderno. El resultado dividió a la crítica y no logró convencer del todo a sus compañeros de viaje ideológicos. Pero hoy alcanza una vigencia renovada y plantea la cuestión de qué fue, en el cine, de los grandes relatos épicos del proletariado. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Fea, malquerida y polémica: el fiasco inmobiliario de la torre más alta de París
items.description: La llaman la torre malquerida. Tiene las mejores vistas de París porque con sus 209 metros es la torre más alta, pero también, dicen los parisinos, porque desde lo alto del rascacielos no se ve su propia fealdad en el horizonte. La Torre Montparnasse , que a pesar de su impopularidad es uno de los edificios más característicos de París, se encuentra desde hace meses en un limbo inmobiliario, pues el ambicioso proyecto para renovarla, que empezó a perfilarse hace una década y cuyas obras iniciales tendrían que haber comenzado este otoño, ha sido rechazado por la mayoría de sus propietarios por su elevado coste: 800 millones de euros. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Mamá, soy rebelde: cómprame una virgen
items.description: Llevar una virgen colgada del cuello es de ser moderna y de ser joven. El catholic-core , la estética de lo sagrado, está de moda y es la razón por la que las adolescentes se adornan la pechera con vírgenes, rosarios e imágenes de santos. Una feminidad que a las mayores nos parece antigua pero que se ha vuelto rebelde. ¿Y de dónde sacan tanta virgen? Pues de los cajones de sus madres y abuelas, de los regalos de primera comunión (las que la hicieron) y ahora también de los centros comerciales que venden rosarios como si fueran Sonny Angels. No hace falta ser católica para colgarse una virgen pero sí un poco rebelde. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Patrick Radden Keefe, periodista: “Vivimos tiempos profundamente mercenarios. ¿Tienes dinero? Bienvenido”
items.description: Radden Keefe está preocupado con el futuro de la prensa libre en Estados Unidos. Reputado periodista de investigación, es uno de los escritores de no ficción más brillantes de su generación. La primera vez que salió de su país durante el primer mandato trumpista, cuenta, no se atrevió a llevarse su ordenador portátil por miedo a que se lo requisaran al volver en el aeropuerto de Nueva York, la ciudad donde vive. “Que yo, como estadounidense que no ha cometido ningún delito, esté asustado al pasar por mi propio aeropuerto, por una policía secreta, un equivalente moderno de la Stasi, es muy preocupante”, apunta, café en mano, el jueves pasado, en un restaurante de Barcelona. Relata que en The New Yorker, la prestigiosa revista para la que trabaja desde hace 20 años, ya están pensando qué hacer el día en que el Departamento de Justicia pueda entrar por la puerta con una orden de registro. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La dana ‘Adam’ dejará lluvias intensas y persistentes en el este peninsular y Baleares hasta el lunes
items.description: Este fin de semana, el tiempo estará protagonizado por el descuelgue y aislamiento de la dana Adam, la primera de gran impacto de la temporada en ser bautizada por la Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet), sobre el norte de la Península. Desde esta posición, y sumada a la entrada de una masa de aire frío y al flujo de vientos húmedos procedentes del Mediterráneo, tumbará las temperaturas en todo el país y dejará lluvias intensas y persistentes otra vez en la ya golpeada área mediterránea peninsular y Baleares hasta el lunes. A lo largo del episodio, “pueden acumularse cantidades de entre 150 y 300 litros por metro cuadrado de forma local, sin descartar valores puntuales más elevados en zonas especialmente afectadas”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Mixta, fija o variable? Qué hipoteca contratar en pleno repunte del euríbor
items.description: El precio de las casas fue el origen del problema. El coste de las hipotecas lo está agravando. La crisis de la vivienda, que ha escalado hasta convertirse en la principal preocupación de los ciudadanos y monopolizar el debate político, abre otro frente: una financiación cada vez más cara y, en consecuencia, una menor capacidad de compra. Detrás de este nuevo escollo están las dos subidas de tipos que ha llevado a cabo este año el Banco Central Europeo (BCE) por temor a una inflación prolongada. Seguir leyendo

items.title: No talks
items.description: THE opposition Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayin-i-Pakistan has announced that there will be no more talks with the government till the latter yields on the one thing it has resolutely sought to prevent: a meeting with jailed former prime minister Imran Khan. Having handed authority for further negotiation to Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai, the TTAP has made that meeting a precondition for a return to the table. If there is any desire among the decision-makers to keep political temperatures in check, the government will take up Mr Achakzai’s offer to reason with Imran. The opposition leader is, after all, a veteran politician viewed with respect across party lines. Unfortunately, it is unlikely that the government is in a reflective mood. It not only managed to dismiss the elected PTI government in KP, but has also had its decision approved by a joint sitting of parliament. That move has poisoned the well. The trouble is that few, other than those who imposed emergency and governor’s rule on KP , are convinced of the government’s ‘security’ rationale, which they see as a fig leaf for an overreaction by the government and its allies, that is unlikely to hold for long: the set-up imposed on the province faces daunting odds. In the four-and-a-half years since the PTI’s government in the centre was ousted, its successors have failed to deliver better living conditions to the people. The people have only heard the words ‘austerity’ and ‘stabilisation’ during this period, and it has often seemed that the former, in particular, has applied only to the public at large, while those responsible for steering the country out of a protracted polycrisis have merely assigned blame and levelled accusations. Every day that passes adds to the public’s disaffection with the mode of governance. The government should understand that the PTI’s protest march and its reaction to it will look like nothing more than a storm in a teacup on the timescale against which governance is measured. It may not realise it, but it has fallen into the same trap the PTI fell into during its truncated time in power. The PTI remained obsessed with hounding its opponents over corruption; the governments that have followed it have similarly consumed themselves with hounding the PTI out of the political sphere. All seem to be missing the big picture — an economy stretched to its limits and a populace experiencing increasing levels of hunger and poverty while outsized egos clash against each other. It is regrettable that the politics of one of the largest, most populous nations of the world has been reduced to single-item vendettas. This must stop. Mr Achakzai has offered a way back to the table, and the government should seize the opportunity. Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

items.title: I sacrificed my dream of becoming a maxillofacial surgeon for politics – Ekua Amoakoh
items.description: Spokesperson for NPP Flagbearer Dr Mahamudu Bawumia and the New Patriotic Party’s (NPP) Health Committee, Dr Ekua Amoakoh, says her involvement in politics cost her the opportunity to pursue a long-held ambition of becoming a maxillofacial surgeon. The medical doctor said she had hoped to specialise in head and neck surgery but had to give up some career opportunities when her political work began earlier than she had anticipated. Speaking in a personality profile interview on JoyNews’ PM Express with Emefa Adeti, Dr Amoakoh said she did not consider the missed opportunity a personal loss, describing it instead as a sacrifice. “No, maybe some job opportunities, yes. So some job opportunities I could not take. I had to make a decision. But for me, I don’t really see it as a loss. I think they are sacrifices,” she said. Dr Amoakoh said her interest in maxillofacial surgery began during her first year in medical school and continued during her clinical work at Ridge Hospital. She described the specialty as a niche field and said she had spent a year at the hospital working towards that path. “That’s what I was doing at Ridge for the whole year. It’s very niche. So that’s what I was doing, and I think I was very interested in it, and I knew even from my first year in medical school that’s exactly what I wanted to do,” she said. She recalled enjoying her work as a house officer and believing she had the ability to build a career in the field. “I enjoyed that. So I feel like if I’ve lost anything, it’s probably my ability to become a specialist in that field,” she said. One of her ambitions was to treat children born with cleft palates, a condition that can require specialised surgical care. “I always thought I would end up being one of those nice cleft doctors, you know, fixing kids’ clefts. I always thought I would be a good doctor,” she said. Dr Amoakoh said she had expected to complete more of her medical career before becoming deeply involved in politics. “If anything, maybe that has been the highest price I’ve had to pay, because I always thought I would be able to get to the end of that before I started. But politics kicked off for me earlier than I expected,” she said. Her comments suggest that the timing of her political involvement, rather than a loss of interest in medicine, was central to the career decision. Asked whether she now loved politics more than medicine, Dr Amoakoh answered in the affirmative, saying political work came naturally to her. “Yes, yes, yes. It comes to me naturally, and I don’t find it really difficult. You know, they say that you find something that you’re good at or something that you love, and you don’t feel like you’re working,” she said. She acknowledged that her schedule had become more demanding but said she remained engaged by the work she was doing. “My schedule has gotten way crazier. But it’s not too much for me because I’m doing things I find interesting. The reading that I’m doing is reading that I would have done anyway,” she said. She made the remarks during her personality profile interview on JoyNews’ PM Express with Emefa Adeti.

items.title: La ley de hace 200 años que sigue decidiendo cómo te sirven una cerveza
items.description: En 1803, el químico inglés William Henry publicó una investigación sobre la cantidad de gas que podía disolverse en un líquido. Difícilmente imaginaba que, más de dos siglos después, su trabajo seguiría siendo fundamental para algo tan cotidiano como servir una cerveza . Y aunque no hace falta saber química para disfrutar de una buena caña, entender un poco de lo que descubrió Henry permite mirar de otra manera lo que sucede dentro de nuestra cerveza. Seguir leyendo
