items.title: Fake Drugs, Drinks, Foods Everywhere: Deadly business killing Nigerians as treatment failures rise
items.description: By Chioma Obinna Imagine getting a new job and being so excited that you buy a bottle of wine to celebrate with your boss. Imagine travelling home for Christmas with a carton of assorted drinks for the elders in your village, hoping to make the festive season memorable. Imagine taking your blood pressure medication every day, only to discover that your blood pressure remains dangerously high. You spend more money on hospital visits, change prescriptions and consult different doctors, yet your condition refuses to improve. Read Also: NAFDAC seizes N200m fake drink packaging in Aba Imagine buying palm oil from the market to prepare your family’s favourite meal, unaware that the red liquid you are about to pour into your pot may have been adulterated. Or buying fruits for your children, believing they have ripened naturally, without knowing how they were handled before arriving at the market. For millions of Nigerians, these are more than frightening possibilities. They represent the growing anxiety surrounding the safety and authenticity of products consumed daily in homes, workplaces, markets and hospitals across the country. But in Lagos and Aba, recent enforcement operations by the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) have brought the danger into sharper focus, exposing suspected operations involving counterfeit drinks and packaging materials bearing the names of established brands. Inside the counterfeiters’ den At Zamfara Plaza, BBA Trade Fair Complex, along the Badagry Expressway, Ojo, Lagos State, NAFDAC operatives uncovered a suspected facility in a two-storey building where alcoholic and energy drinks were allegedly being produced or repackaged illegally. The discovery followed intelligence gathering and surveillance on suspected counterfeiters operating within the Trade Fair International Market. During the operation, two suspects, identified as Chibuzor Okafor and William John, were arrested. Officials reportedly recovered drums, filters, packaging materials, a heating device and other equipment suspected to have been used in the illicit operation. According to NAFDAC, some of the suspects were caught in the act. Speaking during the raid, the Assistant Director of the agency’s Investigation and Enforcement Directorate, Mr Kunle Ojo, expressed concern about the scale of the discovery. “What we have discovered today is a lot, and it’s mind-boggling. We are here to protect the lives of many Nigerians,” he said. But perhaps the most disturbing detail emerged from the explanation offered by one of the arrested suspects. Okafor, who identified himself as a drinks dealer in the market, told Saturday Vanguard at the scene that he changed the bottles of drinks. “I deal on drinks. I change the bottle of the drink. It’s not that the bottle is not good. It’s the drink in there, because the other one is already damaged. So that’s why we are putting it to the next bottle,” he said. His explanation raises a critical question for consumers: what exactly was inside those bottles, and could anyone buying them know whether the contents were genuine, properly produced or safe for consumption? A bottle may carry a familiar brand name, an attractive label and the appearance of a product consumers have trusted for years. Yet those features cannot establish the authenticity or safety of its contents if the product has been tampered with or repackaged outside legitimate quality-control systems. For a customer buying whisky for a celebration, wine for a family gathering or an energy drink to stay alert at work, the transaction may appear routine. The consumer has little reason to suspect that the product could have passed through an illicit operation before reaching the shop. That is what makes counterfeit beverages particularly troubling, the danger may be invisible at the point of purchase. The labels, corks and packs behind the trade in Aba The Lagos operation was not the only disturbing discovery. In Aba, Abia State, NAFDAC operatives acting on credible intelligence raided shops at Old Court Road Market, an area the agency described as notorious for counterfeiting and producing packaging materials for highly branded spirits, wines and other regulated products. What they reportedly found was a large quantity of labels, corks and outer packaging materials bearing the names of established brands. Among the products identified were Jameson, Glenfiddich, Four Cousins, Lord’s Dry Gin and Imperial Blue. Materials bearing the names of Chelsea, Squadron and Seaman’s Aromatic Schnapps were also recovered. The agency further reported finding packaging materials associated with Goya oil. The concern is that such materials, when used fraudulently, can help counterfeiters make unauthorised products appear to be genuine goods from established manufacturers. NAFDAC estimated the value of the counterfeit packaging materials removed from five shops at more than ₦200 million. The operation, however, was not without resistance. According to the agency, traders confronted operatives with threats and intimidation. Some reportedly pursued the vehicle transporting the recovered materials and threatened individuals assisting with their evacuation. The owners of the shops visited reportedly fled, while the affected premises were placed on hold pending further action. The discoveries in Lagos and Aba point to different but potentially complementary aspects of the counterfeit trade, suspected operations involving the contents of drinks in Lagos, and the availability of packaging materials capable of making unauthorised products resemble established brands in Aba. The available reports illustrate why the fight against counterfeiting must go beyond confiscating finished products to investigating the people, materials and supply chains that enable the trade. What could be inside the bottle? According to public health experts, for consumers, the concern goes beyond whether a drink is genuine or fake. It is also about what the product contains, how it was made, whether it was contaminated and whether it meets the safety standards expected of a regulated beverage. Counterfeit drinks do not all pose identical health risks. A product carrying fraudulent branding may contain a genuine beverage that has been unlawfully repackaged. Another may have been diluted, adulterated or manufactured using unsafe ingredients. Without appropriate testing, it is impossible to determine the composition or level of danger of every recovered product. One particularly serious hazard is methanol contamination of alcoholic beverages. Methanol is toxic and, when ingested in sufficient quantities, can cause severe metabolic disturbances, visual impairment, permanent blindness and death. Other contaminants or unsafe production practices may also cause harm, although the nature and severity of the effects vary. According to health experts, improper handling, contamination or the use of unsuitable materials may introduce additional risks. However, it would be inaccurate to conclude that every counterfeit wine or whisky necessarily contains methanol or causes kidney or liver damage. But the Lagos and Aba discoveries, as reported, establish grounds for serious concern about suspected counterfeiting and fraudulent packaging. For the Nigerian consumer, the troubling reality is that a product’s familiar appearance may offer false reassurance. The bottle may look genuine, but the contents and the conditions under which they were produced may tell a different story. Beyond drinks, the danger in everyday consumption Counterfeit products are not confined to alcoholic beverages. Medicines, food, cosmetics, packaged water and other regulated products have also featured in enforcement operations. Products that appear familiar and affordable may be adulterated, improperly manufactured, contaminated, falsely labelled or sold without the required registration. Some may imitate the packaging of established brands, making it difficult for ordinary consumers to distinguish genuine products from fraudulent copies. The problem is particularly troubling when it comes to medicines A patient battling malaria may take what appears to be an appropriate treatment but fail to recover. A person living with hypertension may continue taking medication without achieving adequate blood pressure control. A pregnant woman may unknowingly consume a falsified supplement, while a family struggling to pay medical bills may spend its last savings treating an illness that refuses to respond to medication. In each case, the consumer may have done what seemed reasonable: purchased a product, followed instructions and trusted the system meant to protect them. But what happens when the product itself is the problem? Across Nigeria, concerns about falsified medicines, substandard healthcare products, adulterated food and unsafe beverages have intensified. Behind the counterfeit trade is a public health threat that extends beyond the immediate loss of money. It can undermine treatment, expose consumers to harmful substances, delay proper diagnosis and, in some circumstances, cause serious injury or death. For patients and their families, the consequences can be devastating. For the country, the cost includes avoidable hospital visits, lost working hours, increased healthcare expenditure and declining confidence in medicines and the institutions responsible for regulating them. When treatment fails Consider the Nigerian battling malaria who returns to the hospital repeatedly because treatment appears not to work. Mrs Doris Ibe has taken a dose of it. Doris’s first episode was treated as an ordinary illness. When the symptoms persist, another consultation followed. More money was spent on tests, transport and medication. Eventually, Doris and family begin to wonder whether the doctor has made the wrong diagnosis, whether the disease is unusually severe or whether the body has become resistant to treatment. Yet one possibility Doris and her family may have failed to explored- the quality of the medicine. Treatment failure can have several causes, including incorrect diagnosis, inadequate dosing, poor adherence, drug resistance and complications of the disease. But when a medicine is falsified or contains the wrong ingredients, too little active pharmaceutical ingredient or harmful contaminants, even a correctly prescribed treatment may fail. The danger is that patients may continue deteriorating while the real problem goes undetected. For someone living with hypertension or diabetes, the consequences of ineffective medication can be particularly serious. These are long-term conditions in which consistent disease control is essential. A medicine that does not contain the expected active ingredient may leave a patient exposed to complications despite the appearance of compliance. A counterfeit or contaminated product can also introduce a different danger- toxicity. The result may be a vicious cycle of worsening illness, repeated hospital visits, escalating bills and growing desperation. Families may blame healthcare workers, abandon prescribed treatment or seek alternative remedies, sometimes exposing themselves to further risks. From advertised herbal remedies to dangerous chemicals The risks are not limited to products purchased from roadside vendors or unregistered outlets. Online platforms, radio advertisements and seemingly legitimate sales channels can also expose consumers to unsafe products. A disturbing case reported in Ogun State involved a young woman who reportedly purchased an advertised herbal product from a radio programme in Abeokuta to treat suspected fibroids. According to the account, she inserted the substance as directed but subsequently experienced severe pain and a sensation of internal blockage. Medical experts reportedly discovered that the substance she had been sold was caustic soda, a highly corrosive chemical. If confirmed as reported, the case illustrates the potentially devastating consequences of placing trust in unverified health claims and products whose ingredients and safety have not been established. A woman seeking relief from a suspected reproductive health condition instead found herself facing a potentially serious chemical injury. Her experience raises difficult questions about the marketing of purported remedies, the verification of product ingredients and the responsibility of those who promote or distribute substances for human use. It also highlights the vulnerability of people seeking quick solutions to distressing health problems. When conventional healthcare is expensive, access to specialists is limited or symptoms cause considerable anxiety, an appealing advertisement may appear to offer hope. That hope can be exploited. Experts sound the alarm Reacting to the development in an interview with Saturday Vanguard, the President of the Health Care Providers Association of Nigeria (HCPAN), Dr. Austin Aipoh also described substandard and falsified medicines as a major problem for the country’s healthcare system. Aipoh said treatment failure is among the most immediate consequences. “You have a patient you are treating, and the patient is not getting well. The patient becomes disenchanted just because the drugs are substandard or fake,” Aipoh said. The consequences, he explained, extend beyond the individual patient. Repeated illness can reduce productivity, increase medical expenditure and drain household resources. A family that should be spending its income on food, children’s education and other essential needs may instead find itself moving from one hospital to another, paying for repeated consultations and new prescriptions. “When treatment fails, the patient may lose confidence in the doctor, the facility and the Nigerian health sector,” he said. Aipoh also warned that ineffective medicines could allow illnesses to progress until they become more difficult to treat. “In malaria, for instance, delayed effective treatment can increase the risk of severe disease. In hypertension, inadequate control raises the risk of stroke and other cardiovascular complications. Poorly controlled diabetes can also contribute to damage affecting several organs.” He stressed, however, that these outcomes should not automatically be attributed to counterfeit products in every case. The crucial concern is that a falsified or substandard medicine can prevent a patient from receiving the treatment needed to control an existing condition. The physician also drew attention to the possibility of toxic reactions. He said: “Depending on the ingredients and the extent of exposure, some contaminants may cause acute kidney injury or damage other organs. Other harmful substances may have effects that develop over time.” Aipoh recalled a past incident involving a toxic teething product marketed for children, which he associated with kidney damage and deaths. Such incidents, he said, demonstrate why the quality and composition of medicines and other healthcare products cannot be compromised. He called for stronger regulatory oversight, better reporting systems and improved public awareness. Healthcare professionals, he argued, should have effective channels for reporting suspected substandard medicines when patients fail to respond as expected. Such reports could help regulators identify problematic batches, investigate supply chains and take appropriate action before more patients are exposed. He also advocated stronger local pharmaceutical manufacturing, arguing that improving domestic production and quality control could help strengthen accountability across the supply chain. But local manufacturing alone would not eliminate the problem. Manufacturers, importers, distributors, wholesalers and retailers must all comply with quality standards, while regulators must verify that products meet the required specifications. Aipoh further urged the government to streamline drug distribution and strengthen oversight of the sale of medicines. He called for a need for the government to establish a special court to try counterfeiters of these fake products. Also, in an interview with Saturday Vanguard, Dr Casmier Ifeanyi, a public health expert and National President of the Association of Medical Laboratory Scientists of Nigeria, described the public health implications of counterfeit medicines, food and beverages as far-reaching. He argued that the circulation of unsafe products places Nigerians at risk of severe complications, while raising concerns about the effectiveness of regulatory surveillance. “The public health implication is incalculable,” Ifeanyi said, warning that the consumption of fake medicines, food products and beverages can contribute to complex health conditions and, in some cases, death. Ifeanyi cited the danger of a hypertensive patient taking falsified medication. “If an individual who is hypertensive is taking an antihypertensive prescription medicine and that medicine is fake, the likelihood that the individual will develop complications of heart-related disease, including stroke, is real,” he said. The same concern, he explained, applies to patients taking medicines for malaria and other conditions. A patient taking an ineffective antimalarial may continue to suffer the consequences of the infection, while potentially being exposed to harmful ingredients in the product. The outcome will depend on the disease, the medicine’s actual composition and the patient’s condition. Ifeanyi also raised concerns about pregnant women who depend on prescribed supplements and medicines. “A pregnant woman who unknowingly consumes a falsified product may fail to receive the intended nutritional or therapeutic benefit. If the product contains harmful contaminants, the consequences may extend beyond the mother, depending on the substance and level of exposure.” He warned that consumers with chronic illnesses, including hypertension and diabetes, are particularly vulnerable because they often depend on regular medication to control their conditions. Beyond the physical consequences, he said, the trade can erode public confidence in healthcare professionals and the medicines available in the country. “When treatment fails, patients may wrongly conclude that their doctors lack the necessary expertise, even where the underlying problem is an ineffective or unsafe product.” But Ifeanyi also criticised the regulatory system. NAFDAC under scrutiny Ifeanyi questioned the effectiveness of market surveillance and post-registration monitoring by NAFDAC. He argued that product registration should not be treated as the end of regulatory responsibility, insisting that medicines, food and beverages must continue to be monitored after they enter the market. “The agency should concern itself with the quality and integrity of products that receive their listing and numbering,” he said. He also questioned why consumers sometimes appear to play a prominent role in identifying suspected counterfeit products, arguing that the agency should strengthen its intelligence gathering, surveillance and enforcement systems. “The irony is that it is not this agency that is busting fake and counterfeit food and drugs. It is ordinary citizens, Nigerians, that are discerning,” he said. NAFDAC, for its part, has reported extensive enforcement operations, including raids, seizures, closures of premises, arrests, investigations and the destruction of unsafe products. The key question, therefore, is not whether enforcement activities are taking place, but whether they are sufficiently preventive, consistent and effective to stop dangerous products from reaching consumers in the first place. Ifeanyi called for stronger post-market surveillance, better public education and greater attention to identifying unsafe products before they cause harm. He also urged the agency to improve public guidance on recognising suspected adulteration and verifying product authenticity. For him, the challenge requires a regulatory approach that understands the realities of Nigerian markets, supply chains and consumer behaviour. Treatment failure and the economic burden He advised consumers to seek appropriate medical care and encouraged healthcare facilities to obtain medicines through traceable, reputable supply channels. NAFDAC’s enforcement figures reveal the scale of the challenge Against this backdrop, NAFDAC’s reported enforcement activities provide a glimpse into the scale of the challenge confronting regulators. Data recently released from the agency’s Directorate of Investigation and Enforcement showed that, between January and August 2026, the agency recorded 5,542 enforcement activities, conducted 213 raids, recorded 821 product seizure entries and closed or sealed 179 premises. The agency also reported 52 arrests, 474 newly reported cases, 295 concluded cases and 22 product destruction exercises during the eight-month period. The value of unsafe products destroyed was reported at approximately ₦22.73 billion. These figures cover a broad range of regulated products, including medicines, food, beverages, cosmetics, chemicals, packaged water and medical devices. Also, the volume of enforcement activity points to a substantial regulatory burden. The monthly figures also show considerable activity throughout the period. In January, NAFDAC recorded 232 enforcement activities. The number rose to 423 in February and 673 in April, before reaching 1,076 in May. July recorded 1,089 activities, the highest monthly figure in the reported period, while August accounted for 941. The agency also reported that cosmetics accounted for 401 seizure entries, followed by drinks with 215, drugs with 112, food with 69 and chemicals with 22. These categories demonstrated that the challenge extends well beyond medicines to products that Nigerians routinely apply to their bodies, consume or use in their homes. In addition to raids and seizures, enforcement work involves intelligence gathering, investigations, product assessments, administrative sanctions and referrals for possible prosecution. The destruction of unsafe products is important because it removes goods that might otherwise enter the market. Yet the number and value of destroyed products do not, on their own, establish how many consumers have been protected or whether the overall prevalence of counterfeiting is declining. Those questions require sustained surveillance, reliable market data and evidence of improved compliance. Counterfeiters move online However, the growth of online commerce has introduced another layer of complexity. Consumers increasingly buy medicines, cosmetics and other healthcare products through social media pages, online marketplaces and sellers operating through personal accounts. While digital platforms offer convenience, they can also make it harder for buyers to establish a seller’s identity, verify the origin of a product or determine whether the item being advertised is the one eventually delivered. Director-General, NAFDAC, Prof. Mojisola Adeyeye, has acknowledged the challenge posed by online marketing at one of her press briefing in Lagos where she said the agency had deployed corps members and interns to monitor product sales on platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Jiji, Jumia and Konga. Information gathered is submitted for review and may lead to investigations, arrests or enforcement action. The sale of unregistered or counterfeit eye drops and other healthcare products online has become a growing concern in Nigeria,” Adeyeye said. She said the agency had identified and sanctioned unregistered products, shut down some businesses and handed suspects over for further investigation and possible prosecution. According to her, penalties imposed on some businesses ranged from ₦200,000 for micro businesses to ₦5 million for larger businesses. Adeyeye also said NAFDAC was working with online marketplaces on compliance measures, including the Scan2Verify system and the Green Book, which helps consumers check registered products. She urged buyers, particularly those purchasing eye-care products and other healthcare items, to verify product registration through official channels. The agency has also reported cases in which information gathered online led investigators to physical premises, resulting in arrests and the discovery of additional suspected illicit activities. Yet monitoring online sales presents a continuing challenge. Sellers can operate through multiple accounts, change their identities or move between platforms, while small businesses and informal distribution networks complicate efforts to establish responsibility. She explained that for consumers, an attractive online advertisement, a familiar brand image or a seller’s assurance is not sufficient proof that a healthcare product is genuine or safe. What must change? For the two health professionals, enforcement must be accompanied by reforms that make counterfeiting more difficult and improve the chances of detecting unsafe products before they cause harm. Aipoh called for stronger regulatory powers and more effective prosecution of offenders. He also proposed specialised mechanisms for handling cases involving fake medicines and other dangerous products. He urged healthcare professionals to report suspected treatment failures and products of questionable quality through a coordinated surveillance system. Such reporting, he argued, would allow regulators to identify patterns, investigate products and act more quickly where evidence indicates a safety or quality problem. Also, Ifeanyi, stressed the importance of routine post-market surveillance. A product that meets regulatory requirements at one stage must not be assumed to remain compliant indefinitely, particularly where there are risks of falsification, improper storage, contamination or diversion along the supply chain. The experts emphasised public education. He said “Consumers need to know how to verify regulated products, where to report suspected counterfeits and why medicines should be purchased through legitimate, traceable channels. He said health professionals and pharmacists also have a role in explaining the risks of self-medication and in investigating persistent treatment failure rather than assuming that every poor response is evidence of drug resistance or a more severe illness. Noting that government action was equally important, Aipoh said stronger laboratory capacity, intelligence sharing, effective prosecution, transparent enforcement reporting and cooperation across regulatory agencies can help close gaps exploited by counterfeiters. “Manufacturers and distributors must ensure that products are properly produced, stored, transported and labelled. Online marketplaces must also take reasonable steps to prevent prohibited and unsafe products from being sold through their platforms. “Ultimately, enforcement should be measured not only by the volume of goods seized but by whether fewer dangerous products reach consumers, whether offenders are held accountable and whether patients can trust the medicines they depend on.” The consumer’s dilemma For the ordinary Nigerian, the problem often begins with a simple transaction, buying a bottle of wine, a packet of tablets, a container of palm oil or a cosmetic advertised online. Nevertheless, consumers can take practical precautions. Continuing, Aipoh insisted that medicines should be obtained from licensed and reputable pharmacies or healthcare providers. Buyers should be cautious of products promoted with exaggerated claims, particularly those promising miraculous cures for serious conditions. Packaging that appears altered, missing information or suspicious labelling should prompt further checks. “NAFDAC registration details should be verified through official sources where possible, while buyers should remember that counterfeiters may copy the registration numbers of genuine products. “Anyone who suspects that a medicine is ineffective, contaminated or associated with an unexpected reaction should seek medical advice and report the concern through appropriate healthcare and regulatory channels. Prescribed medicines, particularly those used to manage chronic conditions, should not be stopped or changed without professional guidance. Persistent symptoms also require proper medical assessment, since treatment failure can have causes unrelated to product quality.” A battle that cannot be won with raids alone The reported destruction of ₦22.73 billion worth of unsafe products between January and August 2026 is a significant enforcement figure. It is also a reminder of the volume of potentially harmful goods regulators are confronting. The Lagos and Aba operations illustrate how suspected counterfeiting can involve not only the contents of bottles but also the packaging and labelling that can make unauthorised products appear genuine. Yet the ultimate measure of success is not the number of labels confiscated, buildings raided or products destroyed. It is whether the people behind the operations are identified, whether the supply chains are disrupted and whether consumers are protected from unsafe goods. For NAFDAC, the task is to sustain enforcement while strengthening the systems that prevent unsafe products from entering the market. For healthcare professionals, it is to remain alert to suspected treatment failures, report concerns and help patients access reliable medicines. For manufacturers, distributors and retailers, it is to recognise that product integrity is not merely a commercial obligation but a matter of public safety. And for government, it is to ensure that the institutions entrusted with protecting consumers have the resources, intelligence and accountability mechanisms required to carry out that responsibility. The most troubling feature of the counterfeit trade is that its victims may never realise what went wrong. A patient may blame a doctor, a family may exhaust its savings or a person may suffer complications without knowing that the product they trusted was unsafe. That is why the fight against counterfeit products must extend beyond market raids and destruction exercises. It must reach the point where products are manufactured, imported, distributed, advertised and sold. items.title: ‘It was very difficult to be NPP in 2024’ – Ekua Amoakoh
items.description: Spokesperson for NPP flagbearer Dr Mahamudu Bawumia and the New Patriotic Party’s (NPP) Health Committee has recounted how her research into the party’s health sector record ahead of the 2024 elections sparked clashes with her own colleagues. The medical doctor said her assignment involved gathering and analysing data from the Ministry of Health, the Ghana Health Service and the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) to document the party’s record in the sector. Speaking in a personality profile interview on JoyNews’ PM Express with Emefa Adeti, Dr Amoakoh said she was tasked with using her research skills to develop a comprehensive account of the NPP’s performance in health, tracing its record across successive administrations. “So my first job was to go to the Ministry of Health and collect all their data. Because I came with a skill set, I was given the health sector to do all the research,” she said. She explained that the exercise covered several areas, including health infrastructure and national health insurance, with the findings intended to support the party’s campaign messaging. Dr Amoakoh said the work became difficult amid intense political disagreements during the election year, with some of her fellow party members challenging her findings. “It was very difficult to be an NPP person. My own colleagues were fighting me. And I was like, ‘You people, I don’t understand. I sound like I was in government. I’m here with you people. I’ve just gone there, and you are coming to fight me,’” she recounted. She said the disagreements became so frequent that she eventually left a group chat in 2024 after exchanges with colleagues grew increasingly heated. According to her, the tensions arose partly because the information she gathered from official records sometimes contradicted claims being made in political discussions. Dr Amoakoh attributed the disagreements to the intense propaganda and political contest surrounding the 2024 general election. She said some colleagues reacted angrily when she presented documents that challenged particular claims, making it difficult to have discussions based on the available evidence. “That was in the height of propaganda. It was in the height of the election. There was so much propaganda. And you are looking at documents that disprove something someone is saying, right? But they are so angry that they are arguing with you with their heart and soul and mind,” she said. She acknowledged that she also contributed to the disagreements by refusing to back down from arguments. “So we can be fighting, and one time I realized that, nah, this is getting too far,” she said. Dr Amoakoh said her research went beyond the NPP’s time in government, taking in records from the Provisional National Defence Council (PNDC) era, the administration of former President John Agyekum Kufuor and that of the late President John Evans Atta Mills. The exercise was intended to help the party assess developments in the health sector over time and build a narrative around its own record. Dr Amoakoh made the remarks during her personality profile interview on JoyNews’ PM Express with Emefa Adeti.

items.title: Tesla dévoile son nouveau Roadster : une voiture équipée de fusées qui promet de « voler »
items.description: Près de neuf ans après la présentation du premier prototype, Elon Musk a dévoilé, vendredi 16 octobre 2026, la version de série du Tesla Roadster. Équipée de propulseurs développés avec SpaceX, cette voiture électrique promet des performances spectaculaires, jusqu’à des mouvements aériens. En France, les réservations sont ouvertes avec des acomptes pouvant atteindre 250 000 euros, alors que son prix final reste inconnu. Tesla repousse une nouvelle fois les limites de l’automobile électrique. Elon Musk a présenté, vendredi 16 octobre, la version de série du Roadster, un modèle sportif qui associe les technologies automobiles de Tesla aux innovations aérospatiales de SpaceX. Lors de cette présentation, le constructeur a mis en scène plusieurs démonstrations spectaculaires, avec une voiture capable de réaliser des sauts, des rotations et des figures aériennes grâce à des propulseurs à gaz froid. « C’est mieux qu’une voiture de James Bond » , a lancé Elon Musk, promettant une expérience inédite issue de la collaboration entre ses deux entreprises. Une voiture capable de réaliser des figures aériennes La présentation a débuté par une démonstration étonnante : le Roadster a parcouru une piste incurvée jusqu’à se retrouver à l’envers, à plusieurs mètres du sol, sans tomber. Selon les explications fournies par Tesla, un système de ventilation et d’aspiration sous le véhicule permet de générer une force d’appui suffisante pour le maintenir plaqué contre la piste, même à l’arrêt. Mais la principale attraction repose sur les propulseurs développés avec SpaceX. Ces dispositifs à gaz froid sont présentés comme capables de modifier rapidement l’orientation du véhicule, de stabiliser ses mouvements et de contrôler certaines phases de ses sauts. Real life, baby pic.twitter.com/3QEqn18wig — Tesla (@Tesla) October 16, 2026 Au cours de la démonstration, le Roadster a ainsi effectué plusieurs figures, notamment une rotation dans les airs avant de retrouver une position adaptée à son atterrissage. Tesla a également présenté un saut au-dessus de plusieurs véhicules de sa gamme. Le constructeur affirme que ces propulseurs utilisent des actionneurs entièrement électriques pour ajuster précisément la poussée. Un compresseur d’air embarqué doit permettre de recharger automatiquement les réservoirs haute pression pendant le roulage ou en quelques minutes à l’arrêt. Un 0 à 100 km/h en moins d’une seconde annoncé Au-delà de ses capacités spectaculaires, le Roadster mise sur des performances d’accélération hors normes. Lors de la présentation, Tesla a annoncé un passage de 0 à 60 miles par heure, soit environ 96 km/h, en seulement 0,81 seconde pour la configuration la plus radicale. La fiche technique communiquée par le constructeur fait également état d’une autonomie supérieure à 480 kilomètres et d’une vitesse de pointe dépassant les 370 km/h. Tesla reste toutefois discret sur plusieurs caractéristiques essentielles, notamment la puissance exacte de la motorisation et la puissance maximale de recharge. La configuration mécanique complète n’a pas non plus été détaillée lors de la présentation. Trois versions, jusqu’à 250 000 euros d’acompte Sur le configurateur français, le constructeur propose trois déclinaisons du Roadster : Performance, Thrust et Rocket. Performance : cette version biplace annonce un 0 à 60 mph en moins de 1,6 seconde. Thrust : également biplace, elle ajoute des propulseurs arrière et promet un temps inférieur à 0,9 seconde. Rocket : cette configuration monoplace privilégie le volume de gaz embarqué et annonce un 0 à 60 mph en moins de 0,59 seconde, avec la possibilité d’effectuer des rotations dans les airs. Ces performances annoncées restent à distinguer des résultats qui pourront être vérifiés dans des conditions indépendantes. Tesla précise d’ailleurs que le véhicule n’est pas homologué pour circuler sur la voie publique dans la configuration présentée. Les réservations sont néanmoins ouvertes en France. Pour la version Performance, l’acompte total demandé atteint 50 000 euros, avec un premier paiement de 5 000 euros par carte bancaire, suivi d’un virement de 45 000 euros. Pour la version Thrust, le montant total grimpe à 250 000 euros, dont un second virement de 245 000 euros. Le prix de vente définitif n’a, en revanche, toujours pas été communiqué. Avec cette nouvelle génération, Elon Musk entend faire du Roadster une vitrine technologique à la frontière entre automobile et aérospatiale. Reste désormais à voir si les performances annoncées pourront être confirmées et si cette voiture aux ambitions futuristes pourra, un jour, dépasser le stade des démonstrations pour devenir un véhicule commercialisé dans des conditions d’utilisation clairement définies. items.title: ‘Pakistan among 10 states bearing brunt of hunger crisis’
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan is among the 10 countries bearing the brunt of the global hunger crisis, with climate-related disasters, economic hardship, displacement and shrinking humanitarian funding pushing vulnerable communities deeper into food insecurity, according to a new report released by international humanitarian organisation Action Against Hunger. The report, Ten Largest Global Food Crises, released on Friday in connection with World Food Day, warns that an estimated 10.6 million people in Pakistan will require humanitarian assistance in 2026, despite ongoing recovery efforts and improvements in some macroeconomic indicators. Globally, approximately 177 million people live in the 10 countries where hunger is most concentrated, while acute hunger has doubled over the past decade, affecting 266 million people across 47 countries, says the report. The countries facing the largest food crises are Nigeria, Congo, Sudan, Yemen, Afghan­istan, Myanmar, Bangladesh, Pakistan, South Sudan and Syria. Report sees 10.6m Pakistanis needing humanitarian assistance in 2026 In Pakistan, persistent poverty, high food inflation, rising living costs, limited employment opportunities and declining household incomes continue to erode families’ purchasing power. Unfavourable agricultural prices and broader economic instability have further undermined livelihoods, leaving millions struggling to afford adequate food. As humanitarian needs outstrip available resources, vulnerable households are increasingly resorting to damaging coping strategies, including cutting food consumption, selling productive assets and withdrawing children from school to cope with financial pressures. The report cautions that these measures may provide temporary relief but can deepen poverty, undermine children’s education and nutrition, and weaken families’ ability to recover from future shocks. Limited access to healthcare, nutrition services, clean water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and social protection is compounding the crisis, particularly in rural and disaster-affected areas. Persistent poverty and acute malnutrition remain major drivers of humanitarian needs, while cuts to support services and livelihood programmes are further eroding community resilience. Pakistan’s exposure to climate-related disasters remains a major source of food insecurity. Recurrent floods, droughts, heatwaves, glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) and increasingly erratic monsoon rainfall have damaged infrastructure, reduced agricultural production and weakened livestock-dependent livelihoods. Crop losses and prolonged dry spells have also increased households’ reliance on markets for food at a time when many families have limited purchasing power. Several districts are experiencing prolonged drought conditions, adding to concerns about agricultural output and rural incomes. The report warns that seasonal hardships can intensify these pressures. The lean season from December 2025 to March 2026, characterised in some areas by extended winter conditions and heavy snowfall, was identified as a period likely to worsen food insecurity by restricting access to markets and essential resources. Insecurity and regional tensions are adding another layer of pressure to Pakistan’s already fragile food security situation. According to the report, localised insecurity in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan continues to disrupt livelihoods, restrict access to markets and hamper humanitarian operations. Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

items.title: Chinese FM meets Israeli president
items.description: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met with Israeli President Isaac Herzog at the latter's request on the sidelines of the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia in Baku, Azerbaijan, on Thursday. Herzog said the Jewish and Chinese peoples have a long history of exchanges. The two peoples helped each other during the World Anti-Fascist War, forging a friendship that has become a memorable chapter in history. Israel firmly adheres to the one-China policy and is committed to advancing friendly relations with China, he said. Israel is willing to take the 35th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries next year as an opportunity to expand exchanges and cooperation in areas such as science and technology, investment and people-to-people exchanges, he added. Herzog briefed Wang on Israel's views and position on the situation in the Middle East, saying that Israel seeks peace, not war, but faces threats and challenges to its national security that require a strong response. China has always been an important constructive force in promoting peace in the world and the region, Herzog said. Israel attaches importance to the relevant initiatives and proposals put forward by China, appreciates China's efforts to promote regional peace and stability, and stands ready to maintain communication with China, he added. Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that during World War II, both the Chinese and Israeli peoples suffered greatly from the ravages of war and extended a helping hand to each other in times of hardship, giving rise to many moving stories. Since the establishment of diplomatic relations more than 30 years ago, bilateral relations have developed steadily, and practical cooperation has yielded positive results, Wang said, adding that the key lies in upholding mutual respect, treating each other as equals and pursuing mutually beneficial cooperation. Next year will mark the 35th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Israel and the 10th anniversary of the establishment of their innovative comprehensive partnership, he noted. China stands ready to work with Israel to take the anniversaries as an opportunity to review experience, advance cooperation and consolidate the foundation of public support for bilateral relations, Wang said. Wang said promoting peace and reconciliation in the region is the cornerstone of China's Middle East policy. China has consistently maintained that the Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century and that the two-state solution is the right way to resolve the question. The situation in the region remains tense, while peace and tranquility are still a long way to go, Wang said, adding that the top priority at present is to open full access to the Gaza Strip. The 2 million civilians there must not be left struggling on the brink of survival, nor should the humanitarian catastrophe be allowed to continue spreading; Israel should halt and reverse the forced establishment of settlements in the West Bank, he added. Wang stressed that since the beginning of this year, President Xi Jinping has put forward a series of initiatives and proposals to promote peace and security in the Middle East, which are public goods that China has provided to the Middle East and the world. China stands ready to work with the international community to uphold and practice the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security; encourage all parties to return to the track of dialogue and consultation as soon as possible; and seek political solutions to conflicts, Wang said. Wang said Herzog's father, former Israeli President Chaim Herzog, promoted the establishment of diplomatic ties between China and Israel during his presidency and was the first Israeli president to visit China. The elder Herzog wrote in his memoir that compromises and negotiations do not always result in losing something but often bring about important gains and long-term trust. These words remain relevant and instructive under the current circumstances, Wang said. The Palestinian question is the root cause of the Middle East issue, Wang noted, adding that both the Jewish and Palestinian peoples have the right to live in peace and establish independent states. China believes that as long as all parties remain committed to and maintain their resolve to pursue peace, seek a path to peace by moving toward each other, and stay on the right course of the two-state solution, the peace that people have long yearned for will eventually come, Wang said.

items.title: Croatian president meets Chinese FM, pledges to strengthen cooperation
items.description: Croatian President Zoran Milanovic met with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Zagreb on Friday, expressing Croatia's willingness to strengthen exchanges at all levels and advance mutually beneficial cooperation with China. During their meeting, Milanovic asked Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, to convey his sincere greetings to Chinese President Xi Jinping. China has undergone tremendous changes over the past few decades and made remarkable achievements in economic and social development, Milanovic said. China's peaceful development poses no threat to any country and should be viewed objectively and rationally by all parties. Each country has its own system and principles, and all countries should respect each other's development paths and ways of life and strengthen mutual understanding and trust through dialogue and communication, Milanovic said. Stressing that Croatia and China enjoy longstanding friendly relations and have achieved significant outcomes in cooperation across various fields, Milanovic said that Croatia attaches great importance to its relations with China, and is willing to strengthen exchanges at all levels and advance mutually beneficial cooperation. Milanovic said that he has long paid attention to China's foreign policy and fully understands its positions and views. He reaffirmed Croatia's firm commitment to the one-China policy, stressing that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China. Wang conveyed President Xi's cordial greetings to President Milanovic and commended him for his rational, pragmatic and friendly perspective on China's development and rejuvenation. Wang also highlighted Milanovic's efforts to promote mutual understanding and his longstanding commitment to friendly exchanges with China. With a civilization spanning 5,000 years, China's deep-rooted commitment to peace means that it does not seek to use its strength to dominate others, but instead pursues cooperation and mutual benefits with all countries, Wang added. President Xi has put forward the goal of building a community with a shared future for humanity, emphasizing that all countries should stand together, embrace their shared destiny and jointly protect and develop the only planet that humanity calls home, Wang said. China advocates an equal and orderly multipolar world in which all countries, large and small, are equal and uphold the basic norms of international relations based on the United Nations Charter, Wang said. Emphasizing that China has found a development path suited to its own conditions, supported by its people and aligned with the trend of the times, Wang said that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation has entered an irreversible historical process. China will strive to make the world more peaceful, stable and prosperous, Wang said, adding that China's success is not only its own, but also a success for all countries of the Global South. China is willing to view its relations with Croatia from a strategic and long-term perspective and explore ways to further elevate bilateral ties on the basis of their comprehensive cooperative partnership, Wang said. The two sides also exchanged views on China-Europe relations. Wang noted that there is no fundamental conflict of interests between China and the European Union (EU), and that the two sides can help each other succeed and achieve common prosperity. Regarding the EU's concerns over China's trade surplus, Wang said that the surplus is a result of market demand and the international division of labor. China and the EU are partners, not adversaries, and should pursue cooperation rather than confrontation, he added. Recent progress under the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism shows that the two sides can find mutually beneficial solutions as long as they remain committed to dialogue and consultation, Wang said. Milanovic said that Croatia, as an EU member, adheres to the bloc's common foreign and security policy while striving to maintain its own independence. On current economic and trade disputes between China and the EU, he said that he shares China's position and believes that China's strong competitiveness stems mainly from an efficient, comprehensive system for organizing production. He expressed belief that the two sides will resolve development-related issues through communication and dialogue and find solutions satisfactory to all parties. During his visit to Croatia, Wang also held talks with Croatian Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Gordan Grlic Radman.

items.title: Millions may be forced to move as climate change hits South Asia: UN
items.description: NEW DELHI: Climate change is threatening livelihoods and forcing people from their homes across South Asia, but technology and government action could help limit the damage, the UN migration chief said on Friday. Rising seas, flooding and drought threaten homes and farmland, Amy Pope, director general of the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), said during a visit to New Delhi. In the Himalayas, she pointed to Nepal’s Aug 26 disaster, when a mountain and glacier collapse triggered deadly flooding, where IOM sent humanitarian aid to help. In a worst-case scenario, up to 40.5 million people in South Asia may be forced to move by 2050, according to IOM. Rising seas, flooding, drought threaten homes and farmland, warns IOM chief “When they can’t produce food, when they can’t feed their livestock, it increases the likelihood of displacement,” said Pope. “The first adaptation is often for people to move.” Pope said climate change was also accelerating urbanisation in India. “As people seek shelter from heat, they’re going into urban centres,” she said. Migration as a tool The risks are particularly acute in South Asia, where a vast population and limited resources leave many communities vulnerable. “There’s a lack of urgency globally about the risks that vulnerable communities are facing,” Amy Pope said, warning that funding to help residents prepare for climate change remained inadequate. “The cost of a humanitarian disaster is in the billions. The cost of investing in some of the resilience measures can be far less,” she said. Better data and artificial intelligence could help governments identify communities at risk before disaster strikes, Pope added. “With the advancements in AI forecasting, you can now better anticipate those communities that are at high risk of displacement,” the IOM chief said. By combining weather forecasts with information about local livelihoods, authorities can identify which communities most need help. “If you know a community is at risk, we don’t need to wait until they’re displaced to respond,” she said. Measures could include improving farming methods, training people for other jobs and, where necessary, relocating communities repeatedly hit by floods or drought. Finding the money for such programmes is a major obstacle, Pope said, with governments often struggling to navigate the systems available to fund climate adaptation. India’s investments in early-warning systems, disaster response and technology offer grounds for optimism, she said. But no government can meet the scale of the challenge alone. International migration can also help people earn a living while filling labour shortages abroad. However, Pope warned that growing demand for workers must be matched by safe, legal routes to employment. Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

items.title: Imran being forced into Benazir, Nawaz-style deal, claims Achakzai
items.description: • Demands authorities disclose whereabouts of Sohail Afridi • Mengal says those claiming to be framers of Constitution are ‘trampling it’ • TTAP alliance challenges governor’s rule, emergency before Peshawar High Court PESHAWAR: PTI fou­nder Imran Khan is being forced into an agreement, similar to those given to former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai claimed on Friday. The opposition leader was referring to the arrangements whereby the two former PMs went into self-imposed exile following their respective ousters. Mr Sharif, who was ousted and imprisoned following a military coup by then-army chief Pervez Musharraf, left the country in 2000 following a deal negotiated by Saudi and Lebanese leaders. Benazir, meanwhile, voluntarily went into self-exile after her party lost the 1997 general elections following her dismissal by then-president Farooq Leg­hari. At the time, her husband Asif Zardari was imprisoned over corruption charges, and was finally released in 2004. “The same is happening today with the PML-N and PPP in government,” Mr Achakzai said at a news conference at the Peshawar High Court (PHC). He was accompanied by Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) leaders Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas. He said they were in contact with all opposition parties and would soon convene a multi-party conference. Resigning from the assemblies was also an option, he said, adding that they had submitted their demands in response to the offer of negotiations. “Nowhere in the world is a prisoner denied meetings,” he said, calling for the withdrawal of the “wrong amen­dment”, empow­erment of parliament and the formation of an independent commission to ensure transparent elections. He said no problem could be resolved until parliament was empowered. Expressing concern over the whereabouts of the KP chief minister and other lawmakers, he demanded that the authorities disclose the chief minister’s whereabouts, calling it their constitutional right to know. “We stand with the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The people of this province have the first right over its minerals. Regardless of political affiliation, everyone must unite for the homeland,” he said, adding that they would be safer if the country survived. Mr Mengal said those claiming to be the framers of the Constitution were trampling on it. He questioned the imposition of governor’s rule in KP on the grounds of terrorism, asking whether military operations had improved or worsened conditions in Balochistan. He said KP’s elected chief minister had been removed, while the provincial assembly speaker and a minister were missing. Those who had won the general elections on Form 47 had become members of the National Assembly, he alleged, adding that the system could not continue this way. Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, said lawlessness had reached its peak. “You cannot run a country, yet you have occupied a province,” he told reporters, adding that a cabinet member had himself acknowledged that the system had collapsed. TTAP challenges governor’s rule Meanwhile on Friday, TTAP leaders challenged the proclamation of emergency and imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa before the PHC, seeking to have the measures declared unconstitutional and illegal. The constitutional petition was jointly filed by TTAP Chairman Mehmood Khan Achakzai, Vice Chairman Senator Raja Nasir Abbas, Balochistan National Party-Mengal chief Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Sindh Taraqi Pasand Party leader Syed Zainul Abideen through Advocates Muazzam Butt and Baseem Ahmad Siddiqui. The court was requested to declare the Oct 11 proclamation of emergency, issued under Articles 232(1) and 234 of the Constitution, unconstitutional and without lawful authority, arguing that the required constitutional conditions had not been met or that the measures exceeded the powers conferred by the Constitution. They challenged the purported transfer of the KP Assembly’s legislative powers to parliament and the displacement of the elected chief minister and provincial cabinet. They also sought the annulment of executive orders and notifications that depended on the validity of the proclamation. The petitioners also challenged the establishment of the purported KP Advisory Council and Area Development Secretariat, arguing that these bodies could not exercise powers beyond those conferred by the Constitution or replace established provincial institutions. They questioned any purported suspension of constitutional provisions, including Article 175(3), unless expressly authorised by the Constitution. The petitioners sought annulment of the Oct 11 notification concerning the deployment of armed forces in the province to the extent where it violated Article 245, failed to meet constitutional requirements or exceeded the scope of the provision. They also sought directions to ensure that elected representatives and constitutionally established institutions in KP were not unlawfully prevented from performing their functions and that no elected representative was detained or restrained except in accordance with the Constitution. Pending a final decision, they sought interim relief to suspend or restrain the impugned measures to prevent the displacement of elected institutions, transfer of legislative authority, creation of parallel executive structures or other irreparable harm, subject to the court’s assessment of constitutional requirements and public safety. Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

items.title: Pakistan rules out unconditional talks with Afghanistan
items.description: • Demands verifiable mechanism to end terrorist attacks from Afghan soil • FO says no formal Russian mediation initiative currently under discussion • Warns India that any future aggression will be met with a stronger response ISLAMABAD: The Foreign Office on Friday said that talks with Afghanistan could not be unconditional, while rejecting suggestions that Islamabad was unwilling to engage with its neighbour and saying it would welcome sincere efforts by friendly countries to help resolve the dispute. “Pakistan is not shying away from discussions or dialogue, including with representatives of Afghanistan. Pakistan would welcome any sincere efforts by friendly countries that could help address our legitimate security concerns and promoting regional peace and stability,” Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said at the weekly media briefing. The statement came as Russia recently renewed its readiness to mediate between the two countries, although Islamabad denied the existence of any such initiative. “At present, I am not aware of any separate, formal Russian mediation initiative being under discussion,” Mr Khan said, adding that Pakistan remained open to engagement that produced tangible results. Russia, the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government, has recently renewed its offer to facilitate a settlement if both sides request its involvement. Moscow’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, had earlier this month made this suggestion after the latest round of the Moscow Format consultations on Oct 5 ended without a joint communiqué because of differences between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban delegations over references to terrorist networks operating from Afghanistan. Mr Khan said the absence of an agreed statement at the Moscow Format meeting reflected the Afghan delegation’s unwillingness to accept language on terrorist networks that had been agreed in the previous year’s document. “The fact that no joint communiqué was issued after the Moscow Format is self-evident that Afghanistan did not accept the formulation which had been acceptable until last year particularly about presence of terrorist network in Afghanistan. This shows that there is reluctance on the part of Afghanistan that terrorism is originating from its soil,” he said. The failure to get a joint communique highlighted the central obstacle to normalising relations, which is Pakistan’s demand for action against the Tehreek-i-Taliban Paki­stan (TTP) and other terrorist groups it says are using Afghan territory to launch attacks across the border. The Taliban authorities have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while rejecting Islamabad’s allegations that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan. The dispute has frustrated international efforts to reduce tensions. Qatar and Turkiye last October helped broker a ceasefire, but subsequent round of talks failed to reach a lasting settlement. Saudi Arabia separately hosted discussions, while China held talks between the two sides in Urumqi in April. None of these efforts could resolve the disagreement over terrorist groups and the measures needed to prevent cross border attacks. Pakistan’s position, Mr Khan said, was that dialogue would need to be backed by an arrangement that could verify whether terrorist activity against the country had stopped. “The talks will not be unconditional. Pakistan has been raising the issue of terrorism emanating from Afghanistan at different forums. Unfortunately, the Taliban regime has been taking one step forward and one step backward,” Mr Khan emphasised. “Pakistan has only one demand that there should be a verifiable mechanism to ensure complete cessation of terrorist activities emanating from Afghan soil against Pakistan,” he said. ‘Stronger response’ Mr Khan reminded India of the response it faced during last year’s military confrontation and warned that any future aggression would be met with an even stronger response. FO reaction came after Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh a day earlier threatened a bigger strike in the event of any future terrorist attacks. Singh, while speaking at National Defence Conclave 2026 in Delhi, recalled Operation Sindoor and said that it marked a decisive response to terrorism. He also referred to earlier Indian military operations. “We reject and condemn the Indian Defence Minister’s provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India’s hegemonistic mindset and the risks its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia,” Mr Khan said. “We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a fitting reply to Indian aggression,” the FO spokesperson said. Mr Khan urged New Delhi to draw lessons from the previous confrontation and avoid further escalation. “India should draw an appropriate lesson from the last year’s experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region,” he said. Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

items.title: Desperados, Young Jonn blend Latin music, Afrobeats in ‘Let It Go’
items.description: … Track celebrates self-expression, spontaneous moments By Chioma Obinna Desperados has teamed up with award-winning Afrobeats artiste, producer and songwriter Young Jonn to release “Let It Go”, a cross-cultural collaboration blending Latin music with Afrobeats to celebrate self-expression and living in the moment. The track, produced by Yung Willis, draws inspiration from “Guao Guao”, a reggaeton record created by Desperados in partnership with Venezuelan artiste Micro TDH and Colombian producer Ovy On The Drums. Built around a sample of the original song, “Let It Go” reinterprets its Latin-inspired sound through Young Jonn’s distinctive style, creating an Afrobeats record shaped by Nigeria’s vibrant music and nightlife culture. The collaboration reflects Desperados’ strategy of using music and cultural experiences to connect with younger audiences, drawing on the brand’s Latin roots and the influence of Nigerian music. According to the brand, the song captures the spirit of spontaneous nights out, unexpected link-ups with friends and moments when music brings people together. “Let It Go” is designed to encourage listeners to loosen up, express themselves and enjoy experiences that create lasting memories, while bringing two musical cultures together. Yung Willis, whose production credits include artistes such as Wizkid, Davido, Kizz Daniel, Falz, Niniola, BNXN, Zlatan, Patoranking and Ice Prince, handled the production, combining global influences with contemporary Afrobeats sounds. Rather than recreate the original reggaeton record, the collaboration gives it a fresh identity through the rhythms and movement of Nigerian music, with Young Jonn providing the creative link between the two styles. For Desperados, the release goes beyond music to create opportunities for audience participation through dance moves, lifestyle content and fans’ own interpretations of the “Let It Go” experience. The brand said the collaboration reinforces its association with music, culture and self-expression, positioning the song as a meeting point for different influences and shared experiences. By blending Latin rhythms with Afrobeats, “Let It Go” seeks to capture the freedom of enjoying the moment and the role of music in bringing people together. items.title: First Lady’s RHI extends food outreach to Katsina, seeks community food banks nationwide
items.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA —Nigeria’s First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, has urged state governors to establish functional community food banks in each of their three senatorial districts as part of efforts to strengthen food security and address malnutrition among vulnerable groups. The First Lady made the call while formally handing over food items to the wife of the Katsina State Governor, Hajiya Zulaihat Dikko Radda, for distribution to vulnerable residents under the Renewed Hope Initiative’s (RHI) Food Outreach Scheme. Senator Oluremi Tinubu, represented by the Wife of the Vice President, Hajiya Nana Shettima, announced that Katsina State had become the 30th beneficiary of the scheme, following distributions in 29 states and the Federal Capital Territory. Mrs Tinubu in a statement by Kwapchi Bata Hamman, Special Assistant to the President Media and ICT, was quoted as saying: “Renewed Hope Initiative food outreach has so far successfully distributed food items to 29 states and the Federal Capital Territory, making Katsina the 30th beneficiary “Insha Allah, Osun, Ogun and Akwa Ibom states will be the next beneficiaries of this growing initiative. “Our goal at the Renewed Hope Initiative is to complement the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Bola Tinubu by ensuring that every Nigerian receives the support required, irrespective of their circumstances,” she said. The First Lady according to the statement by Kwapchi Bata Hamman Special Assistant to the President Media and ICT, disclosed that the initiative is sustained by the generosity of two partners, who donate two truckloads of food items monthly, enabling it to support two states each month. . As part of efforts to tackle food insecurity and malnutrition, the First Lady also announced the successful nationwide rollout of the National Community Food Bank Programme, which aims to combat child malnutrition and support pregnant women and nursing mothers. She called on state governors to adopt the framework and establish functional community food banks across their senatorial districts, stressing that federal and zonal interventions alone would not be enough to address the scale of the challenge. Mrs Tinubu said stronger collaboration between the federal and state governments would help expand nutritional support to more communities and ensure vulnerable Nigerians have access to essential food supplies. Katsina State Governor, Mallam Dikko Umaru Radda, CON, described the event as a day of hope and renewed commitment to the welfare of the people, noting that the intervention reflects the Federal Government’s resolve to reach vulnerable Nigerians at all levels. He described the initiative as a practical intervention with tangible impact, complementing the Katsina State Government’s efforts to improve the well-being of its citizens. The Governor noted that his administration in alignment with President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda is working towards building a future where every Nigerian could live with dignity through investments in Education , Healthcare and Agriculture . He added that the state government has made concerted efforts to improve security across communities by supporting security agencies with the necessary equipment to strengthen their operations. Governor Radda further stated that the Renewed Hope Agenda is designed to empower Nigerians to achieve their aspirations, urging the people of Katsina State to support the ruling party in the next election to sustain continuity in governance and development. Hajiya Zulaihat Dikko The Wife of the Katsina State Governor expressed appreciation to the First Lady of Nigeria, Senator Oluremi Tinubu for the gesture stating that the Renewed Hope Initiative has continued to play an important role in promoting the welfare of Nigerians particularly women, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups through its various social intervention programmes. Osun, Ogun and Akwa Ibom States are expected to be next beneficiaries of the food distribution Scheme The food items were formally handed over to the Wife of the Katsina State Governor by Wife of the First President Hajiya Nana Shettima for distribution to the intended beneficiaries. Launched in March 2024 under the Renewed Hope Initiative’s Social Investment Programme, the Food Outreach Scheme offers nutritional assistance to persons with disabilities, widows, and other vulnerable groups, helping to ease hardship and enhance family well-being. items.title: Ablakwa challenges Minority to identify an evacuee denied GH¢5,500 allowance
items.description: Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has challenged the Minority in Parliament to identify a Ghanaian evacuated from South Africa who did not receive the GH¢5,500 allowance, dismissing allegations of unaccounted funds as attempts to create a scandal. The government evacuated Ghanaians from South Africa following heightened anti-immigrant sentiment and attacks targeting foreign nationals in the country. The operation ended on September 4, 2026, after three days, according to Mr Ablakwa. He said his September 7 briefing was intended to provide an account of the exercise to the public. Mr Ablakwa said the evacuation exercise ended on September 4, 2026, and that he briefed the press three days later to account for the operation. He questioned claims that some people on the evacuation list could not be traced and that the funds allocated for the exercise had not been fully accounted for. “All of that propaganda out there that some people on the list cannot be found and that some voodoo analysis they have done showed that there’s some money that has not been accounted for,” he said. The Minister said he had been looking for an evacuee who could publicly state that they did not receive the allowance. “I have been looking for one Ghanaian to step forward and say that when we were evacuated from South Africa, the 5,500 Cedi reintegration allowance I didn’t get it as a Ghanaian. Or the 500 Cedi transportation allowance, I didn’t get it. Have you heard of any one Ghanaian? One,” he said. He questioned why the evacuation had become controversial, insisting there was no scandal to uncover. “So what is this desperate attempt to create a scandal when there is none? When the whole world is commending that all of that propaganda…” he said. His remarks came in response to concerns over the handling of the evacuation, including questions about individuals listed as beneficiaries and the disbursement of funds. The dispute centres on the government’s management of the evacuation and the use of public funds to support returning Ghanaians. While Mr Ablakwa maintains that the allowances were paid, the Minority’s concerns include the whereabouts of some individuals on the evacuation list and whether all expenditure has been properly accounted for.

items.title: L’AES définit ses priorités lors des négociations avec les pays de la CEDEAO dans les prochains jours à Dakar
items.description: L'Alliance des États du Sahel a défini vendredi trois priorités pour ses négociations avec la Communauté économique des États de l'Afrique de l'Ouest (CEDEAO), prévues les 17 et 18 octobre prochains à Dakar. Dans un communiqué, le ministère burkinabé des Affaires étrangères a indiqué que les priorités de l’Alliance consistent à préserver la souveraineté des États, à renforcer la confédération et à défendre les intérêts des populations. Cette annonce a été faite lors d’une réunion des ministres des Affaires étrangères du Burkina Faso, du Mali et du Niger, à Ouagadougou, visant à coordonner les positions des trois pays en vue des premières consultations officielles entre l’Alliance et la CEDEAO. Les ministres des Affaires étrangères, Karamoko Jean-Marie Traoré, Abdoulaye Diop et Bakary Yao Sangaré, ont réaffirmé leur attachement au respect de la souveraineté de leurs pays, soulignant l’importance de préserver les liens historiques entre les peuples de la région du Sahel et le reste des pays d’Afrique de l’Ouest. Ils ont également souligné l’importance de la libre circulation des personnes et des marchandises, et ont exprimé leur volonté d’adopter une approche fondée sur la responsabilité, le respect mutuel et la prise en compte des intérêts des populations, appelant à la recherche de solutions africaines aux défis régionaux. Fondée en 2023, l’Alliance des États du Sahel regroupe le Burkina Faso, le Mali et le Niger ; ces trois pays se sont officiellement retirés de la CEDEAO en janvier 2025. Les négociations de Dakar s’inscrivent dans le cadre des efforts déployés par ces trois pays pour renforcer leur autonomie politique et institutionnelle et définir la nature de leurs relations futures avec la CEDEAO.

items.title: Ahmed Rahhou, un polytechnicien en charge de l'IA et du numérique
items.description: Ingénieur de formation, passé par la banque, l'industrie, la diplomatie et la régulation, Ahmed Rahhou, ancien président du Conseil de la concurrence, rejoint le gouvernement de Fatima-Zahra El Mansouri à la tête du ministère de l'Intelligence artificielle, de la Transformation numérique et de la Réforme de l'administration. Ahmed Rahhou entre au gouvernement ce vendredi 16 octobre 2026, avec la responsabilité du ministère de l'Intelligence artificielle, de la Transformation numérique et de la Réforme de l'administration. Il quitte la présidence du Conseil de la concurrence, qu'il occupait depuis plus de cinq ans, au terme d'un parcours qui a traversé le secteur bancaire, l'industrie et la diplomatie. Né le 25 juin 1958 à Meknès, il obtient un baccalauréat scientifique en 1976, avant de partir poursuivre ses études supérieures à Paris. Diplômé de l'École polytechnique en 1980, il enchaîne avec l'École nationale supérieure des télécommunications, où il se forme jusqu'en 1982. Ce double cursus d'ingénieur forme le socle technique de sa carrière. Il débute en 1982 à Royal Air Maroc, comme responsable du service informatique, puis se tourne vers la banque. Au Crédit du Maroc, il occupe plusieurs fonctions avant d'être promu en 1994 directeur général adjoint et membre du directoire. En mars 2003, il prend la tête de Lesieur Cristal, dont il assure la présidence et la direction générale jusqu'en 2009. Il dirige alors un groupe industriel actif dans les huiles alimentaires et leurs produits dérivés. En octobre 2009, il revient à la banque en devenant président-directeur général du CIH Bank, où il accompagne le développement des services bancaires numériques et la modernisation de l'offre à destination de la clientèle. En février 2019, il est nommé ambassadeur du Maroc auprès de l'Union européenne et chef de la mission du Royaume auprès de la Communauté européenne de l'énergie atomique. Le 22 mars 2021, le Roi Mohammed VI le nomme président du Conseil de la concurrence, institution chargée de surveiller les pratiques anticoncurrentielles, de contrôler certaines opérations de concentration économique et de promouvoir une concurrence effective sur les marchés. Le portefeuille qui lui est confié réunit trois domaines étroitement liés : l'intelligence artificielle, la transformation numérique des services et des organisations, et la modernisation de l'administration publique.
