items.title: FG approves ₦40.8bn health allocation, extends insurance to 90,000 inmates
items.description: By Sola Ogundipe The Federal Government has approved a ₦40.76 billion disbursement under the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) for the third quarter of 2026, combining a major financial boost for primary healthcare with the extension of health insurance to nearly 90,000 prison inmates nationwide. The approved allocation marks an increase of approximately ₦7.88 billion over the previous quarter’s allocation of ₦32.88 billion. The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, disclosed the decisions in Abuja following the 16th meeting of the Ministerial Oversight Committee (MOC) on the BHCPF. He said the decisions reinforce the Federal Government’s commitment to quality, affordable and accessible healthcare, particularly for poor, vulnerable and underserved populations, in line with the Renewed Hope Agenda and the Nigeria Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative (NHSRII). Pate noted that monthly statutory releases into the Fund had increased from approximately ₦8.95 billion to ₦13.08 billion and subsequently ₦20.43 billion. He stressed that increased financing must translate into timely disbursement, transparent financial management and improved health outcomes. According to the Minister, the approved Q3 fund is being distributed across the four statutory gateways according to their required shares. “The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) receives ₦19.87 billion (48.75 percent), while the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) gets ₦18.34 billion (45 percent). Additionally, the National Emergency Medical Service and Ambulance System (NEMSAS) receives ₦2.04 billion (5 percent), and the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) is allocated ₦509.48 million (1.25 percent).” To widen healthcare access, the Minister announced plans to expand BHCPF support from 8,309 to 13,521 primary healthcare facilities nationwide, adding 5,212 facilities across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. To improve access to essential medicines, the MOC approved the operationalisation of changes to the NPHCDA gateway, including pooled procurement through MEDIPOOL, Nigeria’s national Group Purchasing Organisation. The arrangement will incorporate value-for-money safeguards, pricing benchmarks and supply-chain monitoring to strengthen transparency, quality assurance and reliable commodity supply. Following a request from the Nigerian Correctional Service, the Committee approved extending health insurance coverage to approximately 90,000 inmates of correctional facilities nationwide through the NHIA, the implementation will be subject to regular reporting and safeguards, with inmates already covered by state schemes excluded. The Committee also considered a phased financing model to support states in recruiting and progressively absorbing Skilled Birth Attendants and Community-Based Health Workers. To address funding delays, the MOC resolved to establish a subcommittee to investigate bottlenecks in the flow of funds through the gateways, states and local government areas to health facilities, with the subcommittee expected to report within six weeks. The Committee also directed that letters be sent to state governors on the financial requirements for the NCDC to respond adequately to disease outbreaks. On accountability, Pate said the Federal Government was collaborating with the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) to track health sector funds and prevent their misapplication. “Government will not condone any act that is capable of depriving ordinary Nigerians of the health goods these funds are meant for,” he said. Pate commended the Governor of Katsina State for releasing ₦243 million to the State Health Insurance Agency to expand BHCPF coverage and urged other states and the FCT to fulfil their counterpart funding obligations under the National Health Act, 2014. The Federal Government reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening primary healthcare financing, expanding access to essential services and ensuring that public health investments deliver measurable improvements in the lives of Nigerians, particularly the most vulnerable. The post FG approves ₦40.8bn health allocation, extends insurance to 90,000 inmates appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: How Botched Executions Were Handled in Centuries Past
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. The botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two injections of what was intended to be a lethal dose of pentobarbital on September 30, is—horrifically—not unique: As my colleague Elizabeth Bruenig wrote , it wasn’t even the first botched execution in Tennessee this year. The fact that officials tried twice to kill her is somewhat more unusual, but not without precedent. Consider the case of Margaret Dickson, a Scottish woman of the early 1700s. Estranged from her husband, Dickson took up work as a domestic in the town of Kelso, where she conceived a child out of wedlock but hid the pregnancy for fear of being shunned. She testified that she’d disposed of the baby after it was stillborn, but the body was found, and she was arrested. Under Scottish law at the time, concealment of a pregnancy was considered evidence of intent to commit infanticide. Dickson was convicted and sentenced to hang in Edinburgh in 1724. Following what was then the practice, Dickson’s execution was public. She was hanged; her body was placed in a coffin and carted away for burial (by some accounts following a tussle with body snatchers who hoped to procure the corpse for dissection by medical students). Along the way, the burial party stopped for a beer, at which point noise was heard from inside the coffin. The lid was pried off, and Dickson was found alive, though confused. Dickson’s survival became an object of fascination and Dickson herself a sort of folk hero, the historian Mikki Brock , the author of a forthcoming book about Dickson, told me. Authorities in Edinburgh initially sought to rehang her, but they were never able to marshal enough support to do so. Dickson, who came to be nicknamed “Half-Hangit Maggie” (that is, half-hanged ), lived into the 1750s. Or take Joseph Samuel, a criminal who was sent from England to a penal colony in Australia. Once there, he was implicated in the murder of a police officer investigating a robbery. Samuel was convicted and sentenced to hang in September 1803, also publicly. It didn’t go well . On the first try, the rope around Samuel’s neck snapped. On the second, the noose unraveled. By then, the crowd was growing restive; a hasty third attempt also ended with a broken rope. Observers at the scene concluded that the mishaps were a sign from God that Samuel should not be killed, and the governor apparently concurred, commuting Samuel’s sentence to life imprisonment. (Three years later, Samuel disappeared at sea during an escape attempt with other convicts and was presumed drowned; perhaps God’s view was not as clear as it seemed at the gallows.) A third celebrated case was that of John “Babbacombe” Lee, who was convicted of the 1884 murder of his employer and sentenced to die. (By that point, executions in Britain had moved out of the public and into prison yards.) Just like Samuel, Lee was spared by malfunctioning equipment: A trapdoor under the gallows, meant to release the condemned and snap his neck, had been tested, yet it failed three times to open . Lee’s sentence was commuted to life by the British home secretary, Sir William Harcourt, who said, “It would shock the feelings of anyone if a man had twice to pay the pangs of imminent death.” Lee was eventually paroled in 1907. Now infamous as “the man they couldn’t hang,” he wrote an autobiography and was the subject of a 1912 silent film, but he then faded from the historical record. He appears to have died in the 1940s, perhaps in Milwaukee . When I first heard the stories of Half-Hangit Maggie and Babbacombe Lee as a child, I knew they were historical, but they seemed to belong more to the realm of myth or fairy tale. Hangings, mysterious mechanical failures, assertions of divine intervention—all of these seemed like things out of fiction. It was easy to chuckle at quaint details, such as the apocryphal tale that Dickson was required to remarry her husband because she’d been declared dead. And though I’d read about the beheadings of Charles I and Louis XVI, the specter of public execution felt distant enough from modern civilization to be faintly unreal. Now all of these things seem much less remote. Until President Trump reversed course yesterday, the Defense Department planned to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who massacred comrades at Fort Hood in 2009. Pike’s fate is up in the air after her twice-failed execution. Pike, who was convicted of a brutal murder in 1995, has returned from a hospital to prison. The state official who oversaw capital punishment has resigned, and the governor has temporarily paused all executions in Tennessee. Her lawyers have requested that her sentence be commuted to life in prison. The doctor and ethicist Lydia Dugdale writes in The Dispatch that U.S. history offers a grim precedent. In 1946, a 16-year-old boy confessed to killing his employer and was sentenced to die via electrocution. A first attempt failed, and his lawyers sought to block a second. The Supreme Court ruled against them, and he was killed that year. But Dugdale argues that this precedent should not apply here. “From Pike’s markedly swollen and chemically burned arms, to her profound cognitive impairment (the severity of which remains unknown), the state has already inflicted a cruel and unusual punishment on Christa,” she writes. Setting aside the law, “as a matter of sheer ethics, if the state has vowed not to punish prisoners cruelly but has inadvertently done so, the state ought not attempt the same method of execution again.” (In this year’s other botched Tennessee case, Tony Carruthers’s failed execution left him partially paralyzed. He received a one-year reprieve, and advocates have called for his sentence to be commuted.) The historical cases of the men and women they couldn’t hang feel much closer to the present day than they once did. And although some of the visceral details still sound like the stuff of myth, the pragmatic and humane outcomes of these situations stand out more against the backdrop of the recent news. Support for the death penalty has dropped since the 1990s , barely topping 50 percent today. Views are closely correlated with religion—white Protestants are far more likely to back it than any other group, according to polling from the Public Religion Research Institute. For religious supporters of capital punishment, the idea that a failed execution is a sign from above might not be so far-fetched. Among the nonreligious, many people may flatter themselves to believe that contemporary society possesses greater reason and logic than our forebears. Just as we try to understand our ancestors by how they handled cases such as those of Dickson, Samuel, and Lee, future generations will judge our society by its actions. Related: A terrible way to die, a terrifying way to survive The real harm of a public execution Here are four new stories from The Atlantic : Jonathan Chait: Five fabulous days of Katie Zacharia Exclusive: He joined the military. They reported his wife to ICE. How Pete Hegseth’s plan for a reality-TV execution imploded Imagine every AI agent on Earth buying the same cheap paper towels. Today’s News President Trump’s new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia , was fired after less than a week in the role, according to three people familiar with the matter. Her dismissal followed criticism of her first press briefing on Tuesday and questions about her legal credentials. Three children and a teacher were killed in a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, yesterday. Police said that a bystander pursued the 16-year-old shooter into the school and fatally shot him; another child and a teacher were critically injured. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez donated $1 million to support Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign in Michigan. El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers in a race that could determine control of the Senate in November. Dispatches Over/Under : Gamblers are more likely to lose money than make it—yet they keep coming back, Will Gottsegen writes. In the first edition of Over/Under, he explores why bettors return to casinos and prediction apps even when it’s not in their financial interest. The Books Briefing : Don’t listen to the romantasy haters, Talya Zax writes. The best-selling genre is more than just smut . Explore all of our newsletters here. Evening Read Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic Big Tech Oligarchs Have a Terrible Plan for Humanity By Bernie Sanders Should human beings remain in control of planet Earth? Or should we be replaced as the dominant species? As absurd as these questions may sound, and as obvious as the answers may seem, the Big Tech oligarchs funding the artificial-intelligence revolution have responded in ways that should alarm all of us. In Silicon Valley, some of the wealthiest people on Earth believe that they have the power to create a superior species. Sam Altman, the head of OpenAI, wrote in 2017 that AI would allow humans to become “the first species ever to design our own descendants.” What this means for humans, however, remains unclear. According to Altman, we will either jump-start digital intelligence “and then fade into an evolutionary tree branch, or we can figure out what a successful merge looks like.” In other words, humans have a choice: face extinction or merge with machines. “I believe the merge has already started,” Altman added, and is “probably our best-case scenario.” Read the full article. More From The Atlantic Watching for a blue wave in South Carolina What the loss of Starshield revealed How the Catholic Church is rethinking war What three gene-therapy deaths have in common The cutest target of Trump’s D.C. makeover Culture Break A24 / Everett Collection Watch. PS A great folk hero needs a good nickname, which is why Billy the Kid and “Pretty Boy” Floyd endure. Babbacombe Lee—the name comes from the site of the murder—belongs to that tier. I first encountered it on the strange, entrancing cover of an album, a 1971 “folk-rock opera” by the English band Fairport Convention. I wouldn’t rank “Babbacombe” Lee as prime Fairport, but it’s an entertaining listen. As for Half-Hangit Maggie, anyone visiting the Grassmarket in Edinburgh, the site of her execution, can have a pint at her namesake pub, Maggie Dickson’s. items.title: Iran denies Saudi accusation of involvement in Houthi attacks
items.description: Iran on Friday denied having anything to do with attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, a day after Saudi Arabia accused it of having encouraged the group’s recent escalation against the kingdom. Since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July, the pro-Iran Houthis have repeatedly struck Saudi targets including Red Sea tankers, oil facilities and Riyadh’s international airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last week. A Saudi-led military coalition has supported Yemen’s internationally recognised government for more than a decade, and reported on Friday having intercepted more missiles and drones as the kingdom comes under sustained attack from the Houthis. A day earlier, a Saudi foreign ministry official said Iran had “encouraged” the escalation, which Tehran denied. “The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations,” Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement. “Yemen’s armed forces act according to their own interests and assessments, and such claims are not credible to those familiar with relations between Iran and its friends. Nevertheless, Iran does not consider an escalation of tensions to be in the interests of any party,” he added. The Saudi official, deputy minister for public diplomacy Dr. Rayed Krimly, had said the Houthis rejected an offer to meet in Oman at the outset of the latest round of hostilities. Baqaei however reiterated an offer to mediate between the two sides, saying Tehran “has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities”. On Friday, a spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition said it had “intercepted and destroyed three drones in the southern area and Riyadh… and two cruise missiles over the Red Sea”. He added that “in the past hours, we intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile over Yanbu”, a city home to the terminus of a major oil pipeline on the Red Sea coast. The Houthi attacks have proliferated since the group launched a lightning offensive in Yemen in September, seizing strategic government-held territory along the Red Sea coast overlooking a major chokepoint for global shipping. The pressure on Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, comes as global energy markets were already rattled by Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz at the outset of the wider Middle East war in February. – Palace struck – The UN Security Council on Thursday “condemned in the strongest terms continued and escalatory Houthi attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”, as well as their “attacks and threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab” Strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. The Security Council also denounced the group’s “reckless strikes” on Riyadh’s airport, which the Saudi-led coalition said had been targeted at least 20 times so far this month. Krimly, of the Saudi foreign ministry, accused Iran on Thursday of continuing “to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN security council resolutions”. “We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran,” he added. Yemeni government forces have launched a counteroffensive with Saudi air support to retake areas seized by the Houthis, but have so far failed to reverse their gains. On Thursday, the group launched a deadly missile attack on the presidential palace in the interim seat of the Yemeni government in Aden, killing five people and wounding 16 others, according to the health minister. Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani denounced the “cowardly” act on X, calling it a “continuation of (the Houthis’) criminal pattern”. A government minister said on condition of anonymity that Zindani had been present at the time, but “was not harmed in any way”. The minister said the Houthis hit a command centre for Yemeni government forces at the complex with three missiles, and another for Saudi coalition forces with two missiles. Media affiliated with the Houthis said they had targeted “the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them”. items.title: United Nigeria Airlines targets N100bn commercial paper market
items.description: By Dickson Omobola United Nigeria Airlines Company Limited is set to become the first domestic airline to issue commercial paper, with an initial tranche of N20 billion under its N100 billion programme. According to its September 2026 investor presentation, which outlined its financial performance and five-year expansion strategy, the commercial paper will be issued in Series 1 and 2, with tenors of 270 days and 364 days, respectively. The proposed issuance will be the first under the airline’s N100 billion commercial paper programme. Meristem Capital Limited will serve as the lead arranger for the transaction, while Cordros Advisory Services Limited, Coronation Merchant Bank Limited, FCMB Capital Markets Limited, FSL Advisory Limited and Quantum Zenith Capital & Investments Limited will serve as dealers. The issuance comes as the airline seeks to strengthen its financial position and expand its domestic, regional and international operations. United Nigeria Airlines has also secured investment-grade ratings from two rating agencies. Agusto & Co. assigned the airline a short-term rating of A3 and a long-term rating of BBB-, with a stable outlook, while DataPro assigned it short-term and long-term ratings of A1 and BBB, respectively. The airline’s financial performance has recorded significant growth, with revenue rising from N10.3 billion in the 2021 financial year to N90.8 billion in 2025. Profit after tax also increased from N1.3 billion to N23.8 billion over the same period. The airline recorded revenue of N95.6 billion in the first half of 2026. Its August performance also showed an improvement, with turnover rising to N19.4 billion from N14.1 billion in July, while it returned to a net profit of N1.2 billion. The airline expressed optimism that its performance would continue on an upward trajectory for the rest of the year and beyond. United Nigeria Airlines currently operates 10 aircraft, including Embraer ERJ-145s, Boeing 737-800s, Embraer E190s and CRJ900s. It plans to take delivery of six additional aircraft before the end of the year. The post United Nigeria Airlines targets N100bn commercial paper market appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: FG to deploy 3,700 telecom towers to connect 20m Nigerians
items.description: . As Tijani commissions first NUCAP site in Abia . Kalu identifies 16 more locations needing coverage in Bende By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — The Federal Government has unveiled plans to deploy 3,700 telecommunications towers nationwide to connect about 20 million Nigerians currently without access to telephone and internet services. Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Dr Bosun Tijani, disclosed this on Friday while commissioning a telecommunications tower under the National Universal Communications Access Programme (NUCAP) in Bende, Abia State. Tijani said the Bende facility was the first site being commissioned under the national initiative aimed at extending reliable telecommunications and broadband services to unserved and underserved communities. “President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has given us a clear mandate: work towards bringing every Nigerian online. Through NUCAP, we are delivering 3,700 telecommunications towers across Nigeria. Today, we are commissioning the first of these sites here. More will follow across the country in the coming days, weeks and months,” he said. The minister said the project was designed to bridge the digital divide and ensure that geographical location did not prevent Nigerians from accessing opportunities. According to him, rural farmers should be able to contact buyers without struggling to find network signals, while traders should not lose sales because customers cannot make electronic transfers. He also said families should be able to contact loved ones and seek emergency assistance without the difficulties associated with poor network coverage. Tijani urged residents to see the telecommunications tower as an investment whose benefits would extend beyond immediate connectivity to education, commerce, skills acquisition and improved social interaction. Drawing an analogy between the tower and a tree, he said its benefits would grow over time, creating opportunities for farmers to find new markets, young people to acquire digital skills, traders to secure orders from other towns and families to communicate more easily. He assured that the intervention in Bende would not end with the commissioning of the first facility, adding that the Federal Government would continue working with Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Rt. Hon. Benjamin Okezie Kalu, network operators and community leaders to reach other unconnected communities. Speaking at the event, Kalu described reliable telecommunications connectivity as a critical requirement for financial inclusion, education and effective healthcare delivery, particularly in rural communities. He said that although reliable network service might appear ordinary to people who enjoyed it daily, its absence could deny rural residents economic opportunities and access to essential services. “For a rural trader whose payment repeatedly fails, a student who cannot join an online lesson, or a family struggling to contact a doctor, it is anything but ordinary. It can determine whether an opportunity is secured or lost,” Kalu said. The Deputy Speaker noted that financial inclusion increasingly depended on reliable telecommunications infrastructure, as mobile banking applications, electronic transfers and agent banking services required dependable network coverage. He explained that poor connectivity could prevent traders from confirming payments, make it difficult for farmers to receive money for their produce and deny households access to funds sent by relatives. According to him, improved connectivity, combined with affordable services, financial literacy and consumer protection, would help more rural residents participate in the formal economy. On education, Kalu said the facility would expand learning opportunities beyond the physical classroom, enabling pupils to access online lessons and educational materials while helping teachers improve their skills through wider learning resources. He added that young people in Bende would be better positioned to apply for scholarships, acquire digital skills and explore opportunities without travelling elsewhere simply to access a network signal. “The talent is already here in Bende. We must provide the connections through which that talent can grow,” he said. Kalu also identified healthcare as a major beneficiary of the intervention, noting that reliable connectivity would enable health workers to consult specialists, exchange medical information securely and coordinate referrals for patients in remote communities. He further linked the project to civic engagement and public safety, saying residents needed access to accurate information and reliable channels to communicate with their representatives, while electoral and emergency personnel required dependable communication networks. Describing Bende’s location and proximity to neighbouring states as an advantage, the Deputy Speaker said improved connectivity would facilitate trade, movement and relationships among communities beyond the constituency. He, however, disclosed that 16 additional locations requiring telecommunications intervention had been identified in Bende Federal Constituency. Kalu urged the Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy and its implementing partners to work with his office and community leaders to validate the locations, assess coverage gaps and establish a clear programme for extending services to them. He stressed that the success of the intervention would depend not only on installing towers but also on ensuring reliable service, adequate power supply, regular maintenance and prompt repairs when faults occurred. The Deputy Speaker expressed appreciation to President Bola Tinubu and the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy for the initiative and for choosing Bende for the commissioning. He also commended Abia State Governor, Dr Alex Otti, for supporting federal development efforts in the state, assuring that he would continue to collaborate with the state government to accelerate development. Kalu called on traditional rulers and Presidents-General of town unions to protect the telecommunications infrastructure against vandalism, describing it as a critical national asset whose benefits should be safeguarded for present and future generations. The event featured a live demonstration of e-learning at Bende Grammar School using the newly deployed infrastructure and the distribution of mobile phones to constituents. The post FG to deploy 3,700 telecom towers to connect 20m Nigerians appeared first on Vanguard News .

AMA seeks relatives of 65-year-old woman found with severe leg wound at Kaneshie
items.description: The Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) is appealing to the public to help trace the relatives of a 65-year-old woman identified as Aba Esi, who was found at Kaneshie in Accra with a severe wound on her left leg. The woman was found loitering in the area on Saturday, October 3, 2026, and is currently receiving medical treatment as efforts continue to locate her family and ensure she receives the necessary care and support. Head of the AMA’s Department of Social Welfare and Community Development, Felicia Amoakohene, said concerns about the woman’s welfare had prompted the Assembly to seek the public’s assistance in identifying her relatives. She urged the public to share information about Aba Esi widely, particularly through social media platforms and community networks, to reach anyone who might recognise her or know her family. Mrs Amoakohene expressed hope that collective efforts would help reunite the woman with her loved ones. Anyone with information about Aba Esi or her relatives is urged to contact the AMA’s Department of Social Welfare and Community Development on 024 185 6401 or 024 250 2497.

items.title: Guerre en Éthiopie : dans un hôpital de Mekele, au Tigré, des enfants amputés, la douleur partout
items.description: À 10 ans à peine, la vie de la petite Iyerusalem semble détruite. Ses deux jambes ont dû être amputées, mutilées par des obus tombés sur son village du sud du Tigré, État régional du nord de l'Éthiopie, où les hostilités ont repris fin septembre. « J'étais dans l'enceinte de notre maison quand mon frère aîné et notre cheval ont été touchés », souffle-t-elle, le regard vide. « Mon frère et le cheval sont morts. » Iyerusalem gît dans un lit de l'hôpital Ayder de Mekele, capitale régionale du Tigré, reprise le 3 octobre sans combats par l'armée fédérale éthiopienne au Front de libération du peuple du Tigré (TPLF), formation politique qui dirigeait de fait l'État régional et défiait à nouveau l'autorité fédérale. La fillette, dont la jambe gauche a été coupée sous le genou et la droite au niveau du pied, vivait à Qarsole, petit village du district d'Alamata, dans le sud du Tigré. Ses moignons, dit-elle, la font « beaucoup souffrir », mais elle continue d'espérer. « Si je suis soignée et que je peux à nouveau marcher, je veux retourner à l'école et apprendre. » Dans la chambre voisine, Betelhem, 10 ans également, originaire du même quartier, a eu un peu plus de chance. Un appareillage rudimentaire maintient la jambe cassée de cette jeune fille aux cheveux tressés. « Je jouais avec ma sœur quand nous avons été touchées » par une explosion, raconte-t-elle. Sa cadette Melat, 6 ans, blessée au cou, a également été hospitalisée dans le même hôpital. Mais « ma mère était enceinte et elle est morte », soupire Betelhem. – Manque d'anesthésiant « Nous sommes des civils. Nous avons été attaqués dans notre propre maison », se désespère Haftom, le père de Betelhem et Melat, désormais veuf. « Nous n'avons pas d'armes et nous ne combattons pas », poursuit-il, appelant à des sanctions qui, selon lui, n'arriveront jamais, contre les auteurs du tir. « Il n'y a pas de gouvernement », peste Haftom, un commerçant de 39 ans. Trente-quatre personnes ont ainsi été transportées à l'hôpital Ayder de Mekele début octobre, blessées par « de l'artillerie lourde, des drones, des coups de feu ou des explosifs », recense Birhanu Hailemariam, le coordinateur des urgences de cette structure. Vingt-trois étaient des enfants, dont la petite Lomo, 6 ans, dont la jambe droite a été amputée. Un adulte est mort. « Nous n'avons pas de scanner pour examiner les patients, mais nous faisons tout notre possible pour soigner tout le monde », observe Birhanu Hailemariam, qui fait état d'un « manque de produits anesthésiants », mais aussi de poches de sang pour les transfusions. Comparée à la précédente guerre du Tigré, qui a déjà opposé le gouvernement fédéral et le TPLF entre 2020 et 2022, « la situation actuelle n'est pas aussi mauvaise », remarque encore M. Birhanu. « Durant la guerre précédente, les gens avaient des blessures plus graves (encore) et il y avait beaucoup plus de morts. » – Cicatrices Ce conflit, qui a mis en ruine de nombreuses infrastructures, notamment hospitalières, au Tigré, fut l'un des plus sanglants récemment survenus dans le monde, faisant au moins 600 000 morts, selon l'Union africaine, une estimation jugée basse par plusieurs observateurs. Les combattants du TPLF ont abandonné Mekele sans combattre, mais un médecin de l'hôpital affirme, sous couvert d'anonymat, craindre qu'ils reviennent dans la ville. « Le TPLF comme les ENDF (Forces armées nationales éthiopiennes) font souffrir les gens », regrette-t-il. « Le TPLF ne nous aide pas et les ENDF bénissent maintenant les gens avec son artillerie lourde », pointe le médecin, qui dit ne soutenir « aucune des parties. Nous voulons seulement la paix. » Dans une autre chambre de l'hôpital, Hana, 12 ans, dont la jambe gauche est entourée d'un bandage et le visage constellé de cicatrices, ne dit pas autre chose. Le bruit de l'explosion qui a fait « trembler » sa maison et l'a blessée « continue de me revenir à l'esprit », raconte l'adolescente, qui aspire à rapidement « poursuivre son éducation ». Son voisin de chambre prédit cependant un autre traumatisme pour Hana. Sa mère et son frère ont péri dans le bombardement de sa maison, assure-t-il. Mais la jeune fille ne le sait pas encore. AFP

items.title: Borno ADC, Bwala trade words over Zulum’s opposition record
items.description: By Ndahi Marama, Maiduguri The African Democratic Congress (ADC) in Borno State and former Commissioner for Home Affairs, Information and Culture, Inuwa Bwala, have traded accusations over claims about Governor Babagana Zulum’s treatment of opposition parties in the state. The dispute followed a Facebook post by Bwala defending Zulum’s record on political tolerance, which the ADC described as a distortion of the situation on the ground. In a statement issued on Thursday, the ADC State Publicity Secretary, Baba Ahmed Mustapha, challenged Bwala’s position, citing the demolition of a property belonging to opposition figure Atom Magira, alleged threats against opposition supporters, the detention of youths who displayed “Tinubu Must Go” placards, and claims that the party had faced restrictions on campaign venues and billboards. But Bwala dismissed the ADC’s response, questioning Mustapha’s experience in public communication and describing the party’s statement as an attempt to misrepresent his earlier analysis. The ADC said it was disheartening for Bwala to portray Zulum’s administration as tolerant of opposition parties. “Ordinarily, we would not join issues with a former commissioner looking for relevance and patronage, but when falsehood is dressed as analysis, the record must be set straight for Borno people and for history,” Mustapha said. The party questioned whether the demolition of Magira’s three-storey plaza in Maiduguri, alleged threats by the Commissioner for Sports, Youths and Poverty Alleviation, Saina Buba, and the arrest and detention of five youths who displayed “Tinubu Must Go” placards were consistent with political tolerance. It also alleged that it had been denied approvals for campaign venues in Maiduguri, that its billboards had been removed by the Borno State Environmental Protection Agency (BOSEPA), and that some of its members had been profiled. The ADC called on the Nigerian Bar Association, Borno Chapter, the Nigeria Union of Journalists and civil society organisations to speak out over what it described as a shrinking political space in the state. However, Bwala denied that his earlier article was directed at the ADC, saying it was an opinion piece written from his perspective as a member of the All Progressives Congress (APC). “In the first place, what I wrote was neither a letter nor a rejoinder, rather, it was an opinionated analysis from a partisan viewpoint, because I am a stakeholder, as a member of the APC,” he said. Bwala also rejected the ADC’s claim that Magira’s property was demolished because of his political affiliation. He said the Borno State Urban Planning Board (BOSUPB) had issued multiple notices over alleged violations of building approval requirements and encroachment on the right of way. According to him, properties belonging to APC members had also been demolished for similar violations. “To reduce an urban renewal enforcement to ‘opposition witch-hunt’ is mischief, no matter what coloration you try to give it,” he said. Bwala challenged the ADC to publish any court judgment supporting its claim that due process was not followed in the demolition. On the alleged threat by Buba, Bwala said the commissioner had clarified his remarks, which he described as a warning against political violence and thuggery at a youth rally. He said the ADC was interpreting the comments as a threat to attract public sympathy, adding that any genuine threat should be reported to the police. Addressing the arrest of the youths who displayed “Tinubu Must Go” placards, Bwala said security agencies acted to maintain public order during a period of heightened tension. He denied that Zulum ordered their detention and said the state government facilitated their release after preliminary investigations. “I challenge the ADC to prove otherwise,” he said. Bwala also disputed the party’s claim that it had been denied campaign venues and that its billboards had been removed unfairly, urging it to produce documentary evidence of rejected applications and the removal of the billboards. He argued that opposition parties had held major rallies in Borno during the 2023 elections without attacks, and said Zulum had encouraged constructive criticism of his administration. On the governor’s support for President Bola Tinubu and Vice-President Kashim Shettima ahead of the 2027 elections, Bwala said the position reflected political conviction rather than an attempt to undermine opposition parties. He advised the ADC to concentrate on building its structures at the ward level rather than engaging in public exchanges with him or the governor. “Professor Zulum will not be distracted. He is focused on resettlement, security, and rebuilding Borno,” Bwala said. The post Borno ADC, Bwala trade words over Zulum’s opposition record appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Le RCCM, un levier stratégique pour accélérer le financement des entreprises dans l’espace OHADA (Anselme René AIMÉ)
items.description: Derrière chaque investissement, chaque création d'entreprise ou chaque projet de croissance se trouve souvent une question essentielle : comment accéder rapidement au crédit ? Dans l'espace OHADA, une partie de la réponse réside dans l'efficacité du système de publicité des sûretés mobilières au RCCM. Conscient de cet enjeu, le législateur communautaire a profondément modernisé le droit des sûretés à travers l'Acte uniforme portant organisation des sûretés du 15 décembre 2010, en consacrant une approche plus favorable à la mobilisation du patrimoine mobilier comme source de financement. Le système repose notamment sur la publicité des sûretés au Registre du Commerce et du Crédit Mobilier (RCCM). Aux termes de l'Acte uniforme portant organisation des sûretés, plusieurs sûretés mobilières, notamment le gage (garantie portant sur un bien mobilier corporel) et le nantissement (garantie portant sur un bien mobilier incorporel), doivent faire l'objet d'une inscription au RCCM afin d'être opposables aux tiers et de préserver le rang du créancier garanti. Cette exigence est complétée par les dispositions de l'Acte uniforme relatif au droit commercial général qui organise le fonctionnement du RCCM et les mécanismes de publicité légale. Cette publicité remplit plusieurs fonctions essentielles. Elle assure la transparence de l'information juridique, réduit les risques liés à la constitution de garanties concurrentes sur un même bien et permet aux établissements de crédit d'évaluer plus efficacement la situation patrimoniale de leurs emprunteurs. Plus largement, elle participe à la sécurisation du crédit recherchée par l'article 1er de l'Acte uniforme sur les sûretés, dont l'objectif est de favoriser l'accès au financement par la mise en valeur des biens comme instruments de garantie. L'intérêt économique du dispositif est particulièrement important pour les PME. Dans de nombreux États de l'espace OHADA, les entreprises disposent rarement d'un patrimoine immobilier suffisant pour constituer des hypothèques. En revanche, elles détiennent des équipements, des véhicules, des stocks ou des créances susceptibles d'être donnés en garantie. La réforme de 2010 a précisément cherché à favoriser cette mobilisation du patrimoine mobilier en élargissant le champ des sûretés susceptibles d'être publiées et valorisées auprès des créanciers. Toutefois, malgré les avancées du cadre juridique, plusieurs défis subsistent : hétérogénéité des pratiques des greffes, délais d'inscription, accès parfois limité à l'information et absence d'interconnexion complète des registres. Ces difficultés peuvent sembler techniques, mais leurs conséquences économiques sont bien réelles. À titre d'illustration, une banque établie à Dakar souhaitant financer une entreprise de transformation agricole basée à Kolda pourrait avoir besoin de vérifier rapidement les inscriptions grevant les équipements proposés en garantie. Si l'information n'est pas accessible de manière instantanée ou si certaines formalités nécessitent encore des démarches physiques, l'analyse du dossier peut s'en trouver ralentie. Or, pour une entreprise qui doit acquérir des matières premières ou répondre à une commande urgente, chaque retard dans le décaissement peut représenter une perte d'opportunité économique. L'enjeu dépasse donc la seule question juridique. Il s'agit également d'une problématique de performance économique. Plus les formalités de publicité sont simples, rapides et fiables, plus les établissements de crédit sont en mesure de financer efficacement les entreprises. À l'inverse, toute incertitude ou tout retard dans l'accès à l'information réduit la fluidité du marché du crédit. La modernisation du RCCM appelle toutefois une mobilisation collective de l'ensemble des acteurs de l'écosystème du crédit. Les établissements bancaires ont la responsabilité de promouvoir une utilisation accrue des sûretés mobilières et d'accompagner les porteurs de projets dans la constitution de dossiers complets et conformes. Les demandeurs de crédit doivent, pour leur part, veiller à la régularité de leur situation juridique et fournir avec diligence les informations nécessaires à la mise en place et à la publicité des garanties. Quant aux juridictions compétentes et aux greffes, ils jouent un rôle central dans la célérité du traitement des formalités, la fiabilité des inscriptions et l'accessibilité des informations. La fluidité du financement de l'économie ne dépend donc pas uniquement de la qualité des textes, mais également de la capacité de chaque acteur à assumer pleinement sa mission. Une meilleure coordination entre banques, tribunaux et opérateurs économiques contribuerait à réduire les délais de traitement, renforcer la sécurité juridique des transactions et accélérer l'accès des entreprises aux ressources financières dont elles ont besoin pour investir, créer des emplois et soutenir la croissance. L'importance de la formalisation des garanties mobilières ne se limite pas à une simple exigence juridique. Elle constitue un levier essentiel d'accès au financement pour les entreprises, en particulier les PME qui représentent l'essentiel du tissu économique africain. Selon la Société Financière Internationale (IFC), le déficit de financement des micro, petites et moyennes entreprises dans les économies émergentes se chiffre à plusieurs milliers de milliards de dollars. Cette réalité touche particulièrement l'Afrique où de nombreuses entreprises disposent d'actifs productifs, mais peinent encore à les mobiliser efficacement comme garanties auprès des établissements de crédit. Cette situation souligne l'importance stratégique de mécanismes modernes de publicité des sûretés tels que le RCCM. L'évolution récente de l'inclusion financière dans l'espace UEMOA confirme également cet enjeu. Selon la BCEAO, le taux global d'utilisation des services financiers a atteint 73,6 % en 2024, contre 72,3 % en 2023, traduisant une progression continue de l'accès des populations aux services financiers, portée notamment par l'essor des services financiers numériques et de la monnaie électronique. Toutefois, cette progression doit désormais s'accompagner d'un accès plus rapide et plus sécurisé au financement productif. La modernisation des mécanismes de formalisation des garanties apparaît ainsi comme un facteur déterminant pour transformer l'inclusion financière en véritable inclusion économique. Demain, un entrepreneur installé à Kédougou, Kolda ou Matam devrait pouvoir constituer une sûreté mobilière, la faire publier et la rendre immédiatement visible à tout établissement financier de Dakar. C'est à cette condition que la digitalisation du RCCM deviendra non seulement une réforme administrative, mais également un véritable accélérateur de financement, de compétitivité et d'inclusion financière dans l'espace OHADA. Le RCCM numérique de demain doit être pensé comme une infrastructure économique stratégique, au même titre que les réseaux de transport ou les infrastructures numériques, au service de la confiance, de l'investissement et de la croissance. Mais cette ambition ne pourra être réalisée que grâce à une action concertée des pouvoirs publics, des juridictions, des greffes, des établissements financiers et des entrepreneurs eux-mêmes. La modernisation du RCCM est avant tout un projet collectif de développement économique, dont le succès contribuera à libérer davantage de crédit au profit des entreprises et à renforcer la dynamique de croissance dans l'ensemble de l'espace OHADA. Anselme René AIMÉ Juriste Senior – Droit bancaire et Gouvernance d'entreprise

items.title: Naira Depreciation: Onafriq exits Nigeria’s agent banking
items.description: By Juliet Umeh Pan-African technology company, Onafriq, has announced plans to wind down its agent banking business in Nigeria, operated under the Baxi brand by Onafriq Nigeria Payments Limited, citing inflation, naira depreciation and intensifying competition. The company said the economic pressures had increased operating costs and affected transaction volumes, while the rapid growth of instant account-to-account payments had altered the mix of transactions handled by point-of-sale (PoS) agents. It added that tighter margins and increased competition had further undermined the sustainability of its agent banking operations. Onafriq said it entered Nigeria’s agent banking market in 2021 through the acquisition of Baxi, also known as Capricorn Digital Limited, and invested in the business through 2023 to strengthen and expand its agent network. “This investment reflected the Group’s belief in agent banking’s role in expanding financial access and digitising cash-based transactions,” the company said in a statement. However, it said trading conditions changed significantly from 2024, prompting a review of the long-term strategy and sustainability of the operation. Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Onafriq, Dare Okoudjou, said the company entered the Nigerian market “with conviction and commitment” but did not achieve its expected results. “Closing this business was a difficult decision to arrive at, one that affects colleagues, agents, and business partners across Nigeria who poured their hearts and soul into building out the Baxi network,” he said. Okoudjou said the company remained committed to ensuring “honesty, fairness, and a well-managed transition” for those affected by the decision. The planned closure will affect employees whose roles are linked to the agent banking business. Onafriq said it would consult each affected employee and provide support throughout the transition. The company also disclosed that agents using the Baxi payments platform had been transferred to another principal bank. It advised them to move their funds to a principal bank of their choice within 30 days. “Onafriq’s teams are available to provide support and guidance throughout the process,” the statement said, adding that the company would honour its commitments to affected stakeholders and maintain open communication during the transition. Despite the planned closure, Okoudjou said the decision was limited to the agent banking business and did not represent the company’s exit from Nigeria. “Nigeria remains central to our mission, and we will continue to serve the market as a Payment Solution Service Provider through the Onafriq payments network and our card issuing services,” he said. Onafriq said it would now focus on integrating its payments network and card-issuing services into Nigeria’s financial ecosystem. The post Naira Depreciation: Onafriq exits Nigeria’s agent banking appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: MMDAs must commit 20% of IGF to capital projects – Finance Minister
items.description: Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs) have been directed to commit at least 20 per cent of their Internally Generated Funds (IGF) to capital projects that directly benefit the citizens. This formed part of the requirements for preparing the 2027–2030 Composite Budgets to ensure that limited public resources were channeled into projects that improved service delivery and addressed the development needs of communities. The Minister for Finance, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, gave the directive in a speech read on his behalf at the Northern Regional Composite Budget Hearings in Tamale. The meeting was to assess the MMDAs’ performance, review their development priorities, and ensure that government policies were translated into realistic, well-valued, and implementable programmes. During the hearings, Nanton, Sagnarigu, Gushegu, Yendi and Tatali-Sangule MMDAs presented their composite budgets for consideration. Their presentations covered implementation of their 2026 budgets, revenue and expenditure projections, development priorities, ongoing projects, and proposed interventions for the 2027–2030 period. Dr Forson reminded all MMDAs to prepare and capture their 2027–2030 Composite Budgets using the Ghana Integrated Financial Management Information System (GIFMIS Budget Module, to prioritise ongoing and completed projects with outstanding financial obligations before introducing new ones. He urged them to ensure that their budget proposals remained within approved ceilings and reflected realistic revenue and expenditure estimates. He also called on them to strengthen IGF and develop strategies to take advantage of opportunities arising from the government’s 24-Hour Economy initiative. Dr Forson directed that all procurement processes be conducted through the Ghana Electronic Procurement System and encouraged the MMDAs and Regional Coordinating Councils to incorporate relevant HIV interventions into their development plans and allocate the necessary resources for implementation. He said programmes and projects proposed in the budgets must have clear, measurable outcomes that would improve the lives of citizens. Mr Sumaila Ewuntomah Abudu, Acting Chief Director, Northern Regional Coordinating Council, commended the MMDAs for their commitment to the exercise.

items.title: This Saturday on Newsfile: GH₵49.72m evacuation money, EC appointments, sex abuse in schools and Afenyo’s GH₵15m suit
items.description: This Saturday on Newsfile, we follow the money, examine the independence of our electoral referee, demand answers over allegations of sexual abuse in our schools, and ask whether a GH¢15 million defamation suit against a public official has been defeated or merely delayed. First, GH¢49.72 million spent on evacuating Ghanaians from South Africa: missing money or misread records? The government says every cedi spent on the evacuation of 1,964 Ghanaians following xenophobic attacks is accounted for. The Minority, however, says its review of documents obtained from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has uncovered discrepancies in the passenger records, allowances and supporting documentation. The Majority insists the expenditure is fully accounted for and dismisses the allegations. But can the reported number of evacuees be reconciled with the flight records? Do the payment registers account for the allowances supposedly paid to those evacuated? Are the discrepancies evidence of missing documentation, differences in record-keeping, or something more serious? And with nearly GH¢50 million in public and donated funds involved, should an independent audit be the next step? When government says the money is accounted for and the opposition says the records do not add up, who should settle the dispute? Then, the Electoral Commission finds itself at the centre of another political controversy following President John Mahama’s appointment of two new Deputy Chairpersons. The NPP has rejected Emelia Afi Agbenyo’s appointment, citing her previous involvement in NDC political activities and demanding that the President withdraw the appointment. Government, however, has defended its decision, arguing that the appointees are qualified and that the Commission’s composition must also be considered in the context of previous appointments. President Mahama has charged the new officials to work independently and impartially. But is political affiliation enough to disqualify someone from serving on the Electoral Commission? What standards should determine who qualifies to become an electoral commissioner? Can an institution responsible for determining who wins and loses elections command public confidence when its senior officials have histories of partisan involvement? And are the parties genuinely defending the independence of the Commission, or are they applying different standards depending on who makes the appointments? How do we secure neutral referees when the process of appointing them is itself a subject of political contestation? Meanwhile, a JoyNews investigation into allegations of sexual abuse at Obuasi Senior High Technical School raises disturbing questions about the protection of students and the responsibilities of those entrusted with their welfare. The investigation reports that complaints about alleged misconduct involving the school’s headmaster had reached education officials and other authorities months before his suspension. The Education Minister has since directed the Ghana Education Service to suspend the headmaster and requested a police investigation. But if complaints had been made earlier, why did the alleged abuse not trigger an effective response? Who received the petitions, what action did they take, and why did the matter apparently remain unresolved for so long? Were the existing safeguarding procedures followed? And if officials failed to act on credible complaints, should they also face investigations? As the police investigate the allegations against the headmaster, should there be a separate inquiry into the conduct of those who were reportedly alerted? When those responsible for protecting children are informed of alleged abuse, who holds them accountable if the system fails to protect its most vulnerable? And from the courtroom comes a legal battle that is far from straightforward. The High Court has dismissed Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin’s GH¢15 million defamation suit against GoldBod Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi over comments made on JoyNews’ Newsfile programme. The court ruled that the suit was procedurally defective and incompetent. But the ruling did not determine whether the statements at the centre of the dispute were defamatory. Afenyo-Markin’s lawyers have criticised the procedural objections raised by the defence, while questions remain about whether the Minority Leader will pursue further legal action. So, has Afenyo-Markin’s case suffered a decisive defeat, or has a procedural setback simply delayed a determination of the substantive issues? What does the ruling mean for both parties? And where should the line be drawn between robust political criticism and statements that could damage a person’s reputation? When a case is dismissed without the court deciding the underlying allegations, what exactly has been settled—and what remains unresolved? Four major stories, four different tests of accountability. From the management of public funds to the independence of the Electoral Commission, the protection of schoolchildren and the administration of justice, the questions are bigger than the individuals at the centre of the controversies. They concern the institutions we trust, the evidence we demand and the consequences when public confidence is put to the test. This Saturday, join Samson Lardy Anyenini and the Newsfile panel as we examine the records, interrogate the claims, and separate established facts from allegations and political rhetoric. Newsfile airs live on the JoyNews channel on digital satellite channels 421 on DSTV and 144 on GoTV, and streams on JoyNews’ Facebook or YouTube channels on Saturdays from 9 am to noon. Viewers can also follow the discussion by tuning in to Joy 99.7 FM or Luv 99.5 FM on the radio or stream the discussion live on either Google or Apple Podcasts. When it’s Saturday, it’s Newsfile! Newsfile is your most authoritative news analysis programme.

items.title: Marine Police arrest 31-year-old man over suspected cannabis plantation in Volta Region
items.description: The Marine Police have arrested a 31-year-old man, Vincent Lotsu, for the alleged unlawful cultivation and possession of suspected cannabis in the Volta Region. According to a statement from the Volta North Regional Police Command, the arrest followed a routine patrol along the Volta Lake on Tuesday, October 13. During the patrol, officers from the Kpando-based Marine Police unit reportedly discovered a fenced wooden structure at Mangoase in the Central Tongu District. A search of the area uncovered a plantation of suspected Indian hemp behind the fence, as well as 16 sacks of dried leaves believed to be cannabis, which were allegedly in Lotsu’s possession. The police have since handed the suspect and the exhibits over to the Kpando Police Divisional Investigation Department for further investigations. The suspected narcotics have also been sent to the crime laboratory for examination to establish their identity. The statement said Lotsu remained in police custody and was assisting with investigations, with plans to arraign him before court. The Volta North Regional Police Command has meanwhile reiterated its commitment to intensifying efforts to combat drug trafficking and related offences in the region. The Command has also warned individuals involved in the cultivation, possession and trafficking of illicit drugs to stop such activities.

items.title: Syria: Women Barred from Defense, Security Colleges
items.description: Click to expand Image Officials from the Syrian Ministry of Defense hold a press conference announcing the launch of the National Defense Sciences University in Damascus, Syria, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Rami Alsayed/NurPhoto via AP Photo (Beirut, October 16, 2026) – Syrian authorities have imposed admissions rules that bar women from most programs at two new state universities focused on defense and security, with applications closing on October 19, 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The discriminatory rules clearly violate Syria’s international legal obligations and are part of a concerning pattern of actions by the transitional authorities that restrict women’s role in state institutions and reinforce gender stereotypes. The Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research announced on September 30 that admission to programs in law, economics and management, and social sciences at the National University of Defense Sciences is reserved for men. At the Syrian University for Security Sciences, women can only apply to cybersecurity programs. Elsewhere, programs on kindergarten teaching at public universities, some midwifery programs, and the nursing schools in Damascus and Aleppo are reserved for women. “Syria’s authorities are rebuilding the army and the security forces without women,” said Hiba Zayadin, senior Syria advisor at Human Rights Watch. “Women can’t train as officers, and they can’t even study to be the army’s lawyers or administrators. This is discrimination, plain and simple.” A former higher education ministry official told Agence France-Presse in early October that some of the men-only rules predate the transition, and Damascus University, the country’s largest, still admits women to all programs. But the defense and security universities are admitting students through the general university admissions process for the first time this year and shutting women out of most tracks. At the National University of Defense Sciences, at which a mandatory commitment to serve in the military is required, only men can enter the land, naval, and air force military colleges, which teach engineering, and the College of Humanities and Administrative Sciences. The only part of the university open to women, the Higher Institute for Applied Sciences and Technology, involves no commitment to military service. The Syrian University for Security Sciences, the College of Security Sciences, and the Technical Institute of Security Sciences admit men only. Graduates of the university must serve with the Internal Security Forces or another competent body for 20 years after completing college or 10 years after completing an institute program. Women can study law, economics, and social sciences at other public and private universities and can join the police through a separate Women’s Police Institute, which graduated its first class in September 2026. But these new policies effectively deny women a path into the army and security forces. The exclusion is already playing out in northeast Syria, where the authorities refused in August to let the Women’s Protection Units, or YPJ, the all-female component of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, join the army alongside its male fighters. Men-only rules also apply at the state oil and gas and railways technical institutes, whose graduates must work for the relevant ministries, and in the radio and television directing department of Idlib University’s media institute. The restrictions contradict the transitional authorities’ own commitments. The Constitutional Declaration, which President Ahmed al-Sharaa signed into force on March 13, 2025, guarantees equality without discrimination based on gender, and women’s right to education and work, along with their social, political, and economic rights. Al-Sharaa has also publicly pledged to respect women’s rights. Syria is also party to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. CEDAW guarantees women equal access to education (article 10), the right to hold public office and perform all public functions (article 7), and equal employment opportunities (article 11). Syria has entered no reservations to articles 7, 10, or 11. Reserving professions involving care for women while keeping military, security, and some industrial programs for men also entrenches and enforces the gender stereotypes that Syria is obliged under CEDAW to eliminate (articles 5 and 10(c)). Shutting women out of these programs also undermines Syria’s transition. United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 and the CEDAW Committee’s General Recommendation No. 30 call for women’s full participation in all post-conflict reconstruction, including security sector reform. Since December 2024, women have been sidelined across Syria’s public institutions. In the October 2025 indirect parliamentary elections, women won 6 of the 119 elected seats in the People’s Assembly, about 5 percent. The UN deputy special envoy for Syria said that women were consistently underrepresented throughout the process. Senior Syrian officials have publicly questioned or openly disparaged women’s place in public office. In December 2024, the government spokesperson suggested women may be biologically unsuited for some political roles and said their ability to serve as judges “could be an area of study and research for specialists.” Women working in some public sector roles face new rules about their physical appearance. In January 2026, the governor of Latakia, a central government appointee, issued a directive banning female public employees, including school staff, from wearing “excessive” makeup at work, under threat of “legal accountability.” The directive does not explicitly define what counts as excessive makeup or outline specific punishment details. On the other hand, in December 2024, the education minister, Nazir al-Qadri, said the right to education is not limited to one gender. The authorities should honor that commitment, Human Rights Watch said. The Ministry of Higher Education should open the security and defense university programs to women on equal terms before applications close on October 19, 2026, and rescind all other gender-based admissions restrictions. The transitional authorities should revoke the Latakia makeup ban and adopt concrete measures to ensure full, equal, safe, and meaningful participation by diverse women in all public institutions, including the People’s Assembly. Governments and donors supporting Syria should prioritize ending all forms of discrimination, including in the security sector. All Syrian authorities should uphold the Constitutional Declaration and Syria’s international commitments and remove any provision or policy that discriminates against women. “Women are underrepresented in parliament, the police, and some public offices, and are now shut out of the army, Zayadin said. “The authorities have promised to respect women’s rights, but their actions directly contradict those promises. Women’s full participation, in all roles and sectors, is essential to building a brighter future for Syria.”

items.title: Indian billionaire Ambani's Reliance breaks silence on Musk, says Jio awaits same clearances as Starlink
items.description: Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance said it welcomed competition from Elon Musk’s Starlink and that its own satellite services were also awaiting clearance, its first response to accusations that Ambani was blocking Starlink’s India launch. Musk, the world’s richest man, has repeatedly accused the Indian government and Ambani of stalling Starlink’s years-long efforts to launch in a market of more than a billion internet subscribers. India has denied any bias in its approval process. The Friday statement, which did not name Musk, comes days before Reliance Industries’ digital unit Jio Platforms seeks a $108 billion valuation in India’s largest IPO to date. Jio houses Reliance’s telecom arm, which has over 530 million customers and is a potential competitor to Starlink in India’s internet market. “At Reliance, we have never feared competition,” the conglomerate said on Friday, addressing “remarks about Reliance and the Indian market” in a statement it said was intended to “place the facts on record”. Starlink responded on Friday saying it had worked with Indian regulators and the industry for more than five years and had built dedicated systems, gateways and other infrastructure in the country with the required government approvals. “Starlink is ready to connect India with high-speed internet,” the company said on X. In a separate post responding to Reliance, Musk said: “Much appreciated”. India’s long wait for satellite internet Musk’s posts on X have ranged from asking whether Ambani was the “real boss” of India to addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would allow Starlink to compete. The attacks mark a sharp turn for Musk, who has a warm public rapport with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi , and come as New Delhi courts foreign investment and negotiates a trade deal with Washington. India has licensed Starlink, Jio’s satellite internet arm and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb to operate services, but none has the security clearance needed to launch. Satellite broadband could help to connect hundreds of millions of Indians who remain offline, mostly in rural and remote areas. Musk has said he would price Starlink affordably in India to take on Jio’s low-cost internet plans. Cheap data is how Jio built its presence in India, and Musk has used the same strategy in markets like Kenya to disrupt local telecom players.

items.title: Cinéma guinéen : le Rendez-vous international prévu du 19 au 21 novembre à Conakry
items.description: Le Rendez-vous international du cinéma en Guinée se tiendra du 19 au 21 novembre 2026 au Centre culturel franco-guinéen (CCFG), à Conakry. Cette rencontre réunira la sixième édition du Salon du cinéma guinéen et la quatrième édition des FIF Awards autour de plusieurs activités consacrées à la préservation du patrimoine, à la formation et au financement des productions. Lors de la conférence de presse de ce vendredi 16 octobre, les organisateurs ont présenté le déroulement des trois journées. Selon Oumar Kourouma, la première sera consacrée à la préservation du patrimoine cinématographique guinéen, avec des échanges autour de la restauration des anciens films. La soirée sera marquée par une cérémonie d’ouverture, un tapis rouge et des rencontres entre professionnels. Le 20 novembre, le programme prévoit des panels, des master-class et des projections de films, notamment ceux issus de la deuxième cohorte du programme Sabo Ciné Talent. La première cohorte avait permis de réaliser huit films. Le 21 novembre, les activités se poursuivront avec des projections, le marché du film « 224 Makiti » et des sessions de pitch dans le cadre du programme « Ciné Lab ». Ces présentations permettront aux porteurs de projets de rencontrer des producteurs et des investisseurs. Un partenariat avec la structure canadienne Diversity Mosaïque prévoit également la sélection de quatre projets guinéens pour un accompagnement vers la production. De son côté, Abdoulaye Traoré, responsable des FIF Awards, a insisté sur la nécessité de renforcer les échanges entre les professionnels guinéens et internationaux. Cette quatrième édition mettra particulièrement à l’honneur les techniciens du cinéma, dont le travail contribue à la réalisation des œuvres. De son côté, Diariou Sow, directrice du Centre culturel franco-guinéen (CCFG), a réaffirmé l’engagement de l’institution en faveur du cinéma guinéen. Elle a notamment évoqué l’importance de la formation des jeunes talents, à travers des master-class et des ateliers, ainsi que la mise à disposition d’espaces d’échanges pour accompagner les professionnels dans le développement de leurs projets. Représentant le ministre, le conseiller principal du ministère de la Culture a, pour sa part, évoqué les efforts des autorités en faveur du développement du cinéma guinéen. Il a rassuré les acteurs du secteur quant au soutien du département, notamment dans la préservation du patrimoine cinématographique et la structuration de l’industrie nationale. Placée sous le thème « Bâtir une industrie du cinéma en Guinée : identité culturelle, infrastructures et financement », cette rencontre entend favoriser les collaborations entre les acteurs du secteur et faciliter les possibilités de financement et de production des films guinéens. La rencontre aura le Sénégal comme pays partenaire et Kindia comme ville invitée d’honneur.

items.title: Political party head upset over not being appointed KP governor, claims Naqvi
items.description: LAHORE: Without taking any names, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Friday claimed that the “head of a party” was “extremely upset” about not being appointed the governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. “The head of a party is extremely upset over being denied a role in the new setup in KP and not getting the governorship,” Naqvi alleged while speaking to journalists in Lahore. He was seemingly referring to Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who has been critical of the federal government over the imposition of governor’s rule in KP. This politician, Naqvi said, had remained “dependent on the establishment for decades to advance his political career”. “These are the same politicians who remained in politics for decades with the support of the establishment, and this politician even relied on the establishment to arrange air tickets for the members of his party,” he further alleged. He said such politicians had little justification for criticising others now, particularly after having benefitted from the same system they currently denounced. “Political differences are part of politics. But instead of using inappropriate language and making allegations, political leaders should speak on the basis of arguments and facts,” the minister said. Naqvi’s remarks come days after the Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move has drawn criticism from the opposition, including Fazl, as well as Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Raja Nasir Abbas of the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayin-i-Pakistan. In the days preceding the imposition of governor’s rule in KP, political tensions between the Centre and the opposition — including the PTI which was in power in KP — had remained high since jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s party announced a protest march to Islamabad to demand his release. Intense negotiations between the two sides a week before the imposition of governor’s rule had failed to yield any results while Fazl was cast as the man who could defuse heightening tensions between the Centre and the PTI. Both sides had held separate meetings with Fazl, reportedly for his intervention to help break the deadlock in the negotiations. And after the federal government imposed governor’s rule in KP, Fazl accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments amid his efforts for mediation. On Thursday, Fazl again censured the Centre, accusing it of depriving the provinces of their rights. Addressing a rally in Multan, he further recalled that his party had expressed reservations over the merger of tribal areas into KP after the 25th Constitutional Amendment in 2018. “We were not against the merger, but we said that it was an issue of the political future of the people of tribal areas,” he said, alleging that the people of those areas were not consulted on the merger. Raising doubts over the Centre’s reasoning behind imposing governor’s rule that there was a lack of cooperation on counterterrorism, he said the security situation in Balochistan was worse than it was in KP. He alleged governor’s rule was not imposed in Balochistan because the province’s chief minister “praises you”. “In KP, the PTI is in power. […] Where opposition is in power, you topple it. And the resources of former tribal areas, which had become part of the province, you have taken control of them by imposing emergency,” he remarked. During his interaction with journalists on Friday, Naqvi also spoke about the former tribal areas. He was critical of concerns regarding the allocation of resources to former tribal areas. “When the districts … were not getting their rightful share for years, why were these people silent?” he questioned. The minister commented that political leaders had failed to speak out for the rights of the people of the former tribal areas at the time, and stressed that the rights and resources of the people of those areas should be treated as an issue above political interests. Naqvi further said KP was facing serious security challenges , and called on political leaders to play a constructive role in restoring peace and combating terrorism. “Instead of fanning the flames and creating unrest, political leaders should play their role in restoring law and order and eliminating terrorism,” he said, maintaining that the province needed peace, stability and collective efforts rather than political confrontation. Separately, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz railed against Fazl in a post on X. She said it was not expected of a senior politician such as him to support those who facilitate terrorism — an apparent reference to the PTI, which the Centre accuses of backing terrorism. She added it was unfortunate that he was supporting the party instead of “holding those accountable who were responsible for the ruin of KP because of their incompetence, ineptitude and corruption”. She also criticised Fazl for his remarks about Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, seemingly referring to his comments during the Multan address about the centralisation of power. She concluded her statement by saying that no one but the PTI was “responsible for the end of its government in KP”.
